title: ED Technician Competency Exam
blurb: The written competency exam hospitals give new ED technicians at orientation and repeat annually, covering vitals, EKG, phlebotomy, procedures, safety, and triage flow. Each attempt here draws 80 questions from this pool by section weight.

questions.q: An adult patient's manual blood pressure is auscultated at 118/76 mmHg with a pulse of 72. Which finding requires the tech to alert the nurse immediately rather than just chart it?
choices: None of these values require immediate reporting
A diastolic of 76 mmHg
A systolic of 118 mmHg
A heart rate of 72 beats per minute
questions.why: All three values are within normal adult ranges (systolic 90-120, diastolic 60-80, pulse 60-100), so nothing here needs escalation. A tech who reports every normal vital as urgent trains staff to tune out real alerts.

questions.q: A pulse oximeter reads 100% on a patient found unresponsive with cherry-red skin after a house fire. What should the tech suspect?
choices: The probe is malfunctioning and needs replacing
Carbon monoxide poisoning, because pulse ox cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin
The patient is fully oxygenated and stable
Nail polish is causing a false low reading
questions.why: Standard pulse oximetry measures light absorption and cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from normal oxyhemoglobin, so CO poisoning gives a falsely reassuring high SpO2. A malfunctioning probe usually reads erratic or no signal, not a smooth 100%, and this patient is clearly unstable, not stable.

questions.q: Which patient position and cuff size error most commonly causes a falsely elevated blood pressure reading?
choices: Cuff too large for the arm, arm at heart level
Cuff placed over a thin shirt sleeve
Cuff too small for the arm, arm hanging unsupported below heart level
Patient legs crossed with cuff sized correctly
questions.why: An undersized cuff needs more pressure to occlude the brachial artery, and an unsupported arm below heart level adds hydrostatic pressure, both falsely raising the reading. An oversized cuff falsely lowers pressure, and legs crossed is a smaller, secondary source of error.

questions.q: An ED tech obtains orthostatic vital signs. After 2 minutes standing, the patient's heart rate rises from 78 to 115 and systolic BP drops from 122 to 98. How should this be interpreted?
choices: Normal orthostatic response, no action needed
This only matters in patients over 65
The cuff was applied incorrectly
A positive orthostatic test suggesting volume depletion; report it
questions.why: A positive orthostatic result is generally a heart rate increase of 30 or more, or a systolic drop of 20 mmHg or more (or diastolic drop of 10), on standing; both criteria are met here and suggest volume depletion that needs prompt reporting, not a repeat measurement first.

questions.q: Where should the pulse oximeter probe NOT be relied upon for an accurate reading?
choices: A cold, vasoconstricted finger with poor perfusion or nail polish on the digit
An earlobe with good capillary refill
The index finger of a warm, well-perfused hand
The toe of a pediatric patient with no polish
questions.why: Poor peripheral perfusion (cold extremities, shock, hypotension) and dark nail polish or acrylics can block or distort the light absorption the sensor depends on, producing unreliable readings. Warm fingers, clean earlobes, and pediatric toes without polish are all acceptable sites.

questions.q: A febrile 4-year-old has a temporal artery temperature of 39.4°C (102.9°F). What is the most appropriate next step for the tech?
choices: Chart it and move on, this is normal for a toddler
Report the fever per protocol and prepare for possible antipyretic order or further workup
Recheck rectally only if the child looks well
Assume the thermometer is broken since it's higher than an axillary would read
questions.why: A significant fever in a young child should be reported so the team can assess for source and consider antipyretics or further workup; it is not something to simply chart without notifying anyone. Temporal readings run close to core temperature, not falsely high, so equipment failure isn't the first assumption.

questions.q: Which vital sign route is generally considered the most accurate reflection of core body temperature in a hemodynamically unstable patient?
choices: Oral
Axillary
Rectal or an internal (bladder/esophageal) probe when available
Tympanic
questions.why: Rectal and internal core probes correlate most closely with true core temperature, especially important when perfusion is poor and peripheral routes become unreliable. Oral, axillary, and tympanic readings are more affected by ambient temperature, mouth breathing, or ear canal debris.

questions.q: A telemetry patient's monitor shows a heart rate of 42 with new-onset dizziness and diaphoresis. What is the tech's correct first action?
choices: Silence the alarm since bradycardia isn't dangerous
Ask the patient to walk to the bathroom to see if it resolves
Document the rhythm and reassess in one hour
Immediately notify the nurse or provider and stay with the patient
questions.why: Symptomatic bradycardia (dizziness, diaphoresis) paired with a rate this low is an unstable finding that needs immediate escalation and continuous observation, not a delayed reassessment. Silencing the alarm or having the patient ambulate could let a dangerous rhythm go unaddressed.

questions.q: Using the 0-10 numeric pain scale, a patient rates abdominal pain a 9 but is calmly texting on their phone and shows no distress behaviors. What should the tech do?
choices: Document the patient's stated number as reported; self-report is the standard, and note behavioral observations separately
Assume the patient is exaggerating and chart a lower number
Refuse to document until the patient 'acts like' a 9
Round the score down to match observed behavior
questions.why: Pain is subjective, and self-report using a validated scale is the gold standard regardless of how calm the patient appears; behavior alone does not override the patient's stated number. The tech should document both the number given and objective observations, not substitute a personal judgment for the reported score.

questions.q: For adult telemetry monitoring, correct placement of the right arm (white) lead is:
choices: Left upper chest, below the clavicle
Right upper chest, below the clavicle
Right lower abdomen
Left lower rib margin
questions.why: Standard 4- or 5-lead limb placement puts white (RA) on the right upper chest below the clavicle, black (LA) on the left upper chest, and the leg leads lower on each side (red/RL, green or LL depending on system). Reversing arm leads is a classic cause of monitor artifact that mimics rhythm changes.

questions.q: A normal resting heart rate range for a healthy adult at rest is generally accepted as:
choices: 40-60 beats per minute
100-120 beats per minute
60-100 beats per minute
50-90 beats per minute
questions.why: 60-100 bpm is the standard adult normal range used in most US clinical settings; rates below 60 (bradycardia) or above 100 (tachycardia) outside of a trained athlete's baseline warrant closer attention and documentation.

questions.q: A neonate's respiratory rate is measured at 58 breaths per minute at rest. This is:
choices: Abnormally high and must be reported immediately
Indicative of respiratory distress requiring oxygen
Only normal if the infant is crying
Within the normal newborn range of roughly 30-60 breaths per minute
questions.why: Newborn respiratory rates normally run 30-60 breaths per minute, faster than older children and adults, so 58 alone is not alarming. It becomes concerning when paired with grunting, retractions, nasal flaring, or sustained rates outside that range, not from the number in isolation.

questions.q: Which statement about manual blood pressure technique is correct?
choices: The stethoscope diaphragm should be placed over the antecubital brachial artery, cuff inflated 20-30 mmHg above the point the palpated pulse disappears
The cuff should always be inflated to 250 mmHg regardless of patient
Korotkoff sounds are irrelevant to obtaining an accurate reading
The bladder of the cuff should cover less than 40% of the arm circumference
questions.why: Correct technique inflates the cuff 20-30 mmHg past the palpated occlusion point to avoid missing an auscultatory gap, with the cuff bladder covering about 80% of the arm circumference, not less than 40%. A fixed 250 mmHg for every patient risks unnecessary discomfort and is not standard.

questions.q: A patient's SpO2 reads 88% on room air but the patient is talking in full sentences with no distress. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Ignore the reading since the patient looks fine
Report the low reading; hypoxemia at this level requires evaluation even without obvious symptoms
Wait until the patient becomes symptomatic before reporting
Recheck in 4 hours as part of routine vitals
questions.why: An SpO2 of 88% is significantly below the normal 94-100% range and needs prompt reporting regardless of how the patient appears, since compensation can mask early hypoxemia. Waiting for visible distress risks missing a deteriorating patient.

questions.q: The correct technique for an oral temperature measurement requires waiting how long after the patient has had hot or cold liquids or smoked, to avoid a false reading?
choices: No waiting period is needed
About 5 minutes is always sufficient
About 15-30 minutes
2 hours minimum
questions.why: Hot or cold intake, and smoking, can transiently change oral mucosal temperature, so guidance is to wait roughly 15-30 minutes before taking an accurate oral temperature. Skipping the wait or only waiting 5 minutes risks a skewed reading.

questions.q: A pediatric patient's blood pressure cuff is chosen based on:
choices: The child's age only
Weight only, regardless of arm size
Whatever cuff is closest on the cart
Arm circumference, with the bladder width about 40% of the arm circumference and length covering 80-100%
questions.why: Cuff sizing is based on the limb's actual circumference, not age or weight alone, because body proportions vary widely between children. An incorrectly sized cuff (too small or too large) skews the reading the same way it does in adults.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes 'orthostatic vital signs' testing?
choices: Comparing BP and HR supine or sitting, then again after standing (or sitting) for 1-3 minutes, watching for a significant rise in HR or drop in BP
Taking BP and HR once while the patient is supine only
Taking a temperature before and after ambulation
Checking pulse ox with the patient lying on each side
questions.why: Orthostatics compare vitals between a resting position and after a position change (typically standing 1-3 minutes), specifically looking for a heart rate rise of 30+ or systolic drop of 20+ mmHg that suggests volume depletion or autonomic dysfunction.

questions.q: A patient on a 5-lead telemetry system has a lead fall off, and the monitor shows a flatline with no alarm pattern consistent with the patient's appearance (awake, talking). The tech's first move should be:
choices: Call a code immediately without checking the patient
Look at the patient and check the lead/electrode connections before assuming a true asystole
Silence the alarm permanently
Assume the monitor is broken and ignore it for the shift
questions.why: Always assess the actual patient first; a disconnected lead or dislodged electrode is a far more common cause of a flatline artifact than true asystole in an alert, talking patient. Calling a code on artifact alone, or permanently silencing alarms, both create patient safety risks.

questions.q: Normal adult respiratory rate at rest is generally:
choices: 8-10 breaths per minute
24-30 breaths per minute
12-20 breaths per minute
30-40 breaths per minute
questions.why: 12-20 breaths per minute is the accepted adult resting range; rates below 12 (bradypnea) or above 20 (tachypnea) should prompt closer assessment, especially paired with abnormal SpO2 or mental status changes.

questions.q: A patient's temperature is documented as 38.9°C. Converted to Fahrenheit, roughly, this is:
questions.why: Using F = (C x 9/5) + 32, 38.9°C converts to about 102.0°F, a significant fever that should be reported per protocol, not a normal or mildly elevated value.

questions.q: When taking a blood pressure on a patient with a fistula for dialysis in the left arm, the tech should:
choices: Take the BP in the right arm (or per facility policy, thigh) and avoid the fistula arm entirely
Use the left arm since it's more accessible
Use the left arm but apply the cuff below the fistula
Ask the patient to make a fist during a left-arm reading to compensate
questions.why: Cuff pressure on a fistula or graft arm can damage the vascular access needed for dialysis, so BP should be taken on the unaffected arm; this is a hard rule, not something modified by cuff placement location on the same arm.

questions.q: A patient's pulse is described as 'thready.' This term means:
choices: Strong, bounding, and easy to palpate
Weak and rapid, difficult to palpate, often signaling poor perfusion
Perfectly normal in tone and rate
An irregular but strong pulse
questions.why: A thready pulse is weak, often rapid, and hard to feel, classically associated with hypovolemia or shock states where stroke volume and perfusion are reduced; it is a concerning finding that should be reported, not a normal variant.

questions.q: The 'fifth vital sign' commonly referred to in ED workflow is:
choices: Skin color
Capillary refill
Pain level
Level of consciousness
questions.why: Pain is widely referred to as the fifth vital sign, assessed and documented alongside temperature, pulse, respirations, and blood pressure using a standardized scale appropriate to the patient's age and ability to communicate.

questions.q: Capillary refill time greater than how many seconds is generally considered delayed/abnormal in an adult?
choices: 1 second
6 seconds
4 seconds
2 seconds
questions.why: A capillary refill time of more than about 2 seconds is generally considered delayed and can indicate poor peripheral perfusion; it should prompt a broader assessment of perfusion status, including vitals and skin findings.

questions.q: A tech notices a patient's blood pressure cuff was applied over a rolled-up sleeve. What error does this most likely cause?
choices: A falsely elevated reading due to a tourniquet-like constriction effect from the bunched fabric
No effect on accuracy
A falsely low reading only
Only affects heart rate, not blood pressure
questions.why: A rolled or bunched sleeve under the cuff can act like a tourniquet and also prevents proper cuff-to-limb contact, both of which tend to falsely elevate the reading; the cuff should be applied to bare skin or a single thin layer of clothing per protocol.

questions.q: Which combination of vital sign changes is most consistent with early compensated shock?
choices: Bradycardia, hypertension, warm skin
Tachycardia, narrowing pulse pressure, cool/clammy skin, normal or slightly low blood pressure
Normal heart rate, wide pulse pressure, flushed skin
Bradypnea, bradycardia, warm dry skin
questions.why: Early compensated shock shows tachycardia and vasoconstriction (cool, clammy skin) as the body maintains blood pressure by increasing heart rate and systemic vascular resistance; blood pressure itself may still look normal, making heart rate and skin signs the earlier clues.

questions.q: An ED tech is asked to obtain a set of vitals on a patient in 4-point restraints. In addition to standard vitals, what specific monitoring is required?
choices: Nothing additional; standard vitals are sufficient
Only a pain score is needed
Circulation, sensation, and movement (neurovascular checks) of the restrained extremities at facility-specified intervals
Restrained patients do not need vitals since they are being closely watched anyway
questions.why: Restrained patients require regular neurovascular checks (circulation, sensation, movement) of each restrained limb in addition to vital signs, documented at the intervals set by policy, because restraints themselves carry a risk of impaired circulation or nerve injury.

questions.q: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is composed of which three components?
choices: Pulse, respirations, blood pressure
Temperature, pain score, oxygen saturation
Pupil size, skin color, capillary refill
Eye opening, verbal response, motor response
questions.why: GCS totals eye opening (max 4), verbal response (max 5), and motor response (max 6) for a maximum score of 15; it is a standardized way to communicate level of consciousness and track neurological changes over time.

questions.q: A patient's oxygen saturation is 91% and they are on 2L nasal cannula. The tech should:
choices: Report the finding to the nurse/provider; oxygen device and flow changes require an order in most EDs
Increase the flow rate on their own without an order
Remove the cannula since it isn't working
Assume the pulse ox is defective
questions.why: Even though hypoxemia needs prompt reporting, changing supplemental oxygen delivery or flow is typically outside tech scope and requires a nurse or provider order, except in specific protocol-driven or emergent situations defined by the facility.

questions.q: Which of these is a common cause of a falsely low pulse oximetry reading?
choices: Well-perfused warm extremity
Nail polish, especially dark blue, black, or green shades
Bright ambient lighting in a well-lit room
Patient breathing room air normally
questions.why: Dark nail polish (especially blue, black, or green) can absorb light in a way that interferes with the sensor and falsely lowers the reading; clear or light polish generally has minimal effect. A warm, well-perfused extremity and normal room air breathing do not cause false lows.

questions.q: A tech is asked to obtain a 'set of vitals' on a triage patient. This standard set typically includes:
choices: Only pulse and blood pressure
Only pulse oximetry and pain score
Temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry (with pain score as the fifth vital sign)
Blood pressure and temperature only
questions.why: A complete standard vital sign set in most EDs includes temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and SpO2, with a pain score commonly added; omitting any of these can miss an important clinical clue at triage.

questions.q: A patient's blood pressure is 152/94 on the first reading. What is the appropriate next step before reporting it as abnormal?
choices: Report immediately without rechecking
Take the BP standing only, ignore sitting or supine values
Assume it's 'white coat' anxiety and disregard it
Recheck after the patient has rested a few minutes, using proper technique and correct cuff size, before treating a single reading as definitive
questions.why: A single elevated reading can be affected by anxiety, recent activity, improper cuff size, or unsupported arm position, so best practice is to recheck with correct technique before treating it as the patient's true value; this doesn't mean ignoring or delaying appropriate reporting once confirmed.

questions.q: Which pediatric vital sign finding should be reported immediately as a red flag?
choices: Respiratory rate of 60 with grunting and nasal flaring in an infant
Heart rate of 110 in a 2-year-old at rest
Temperature of 37.2°C in a toddler
Heart rate of 90 in a sleeping 8-year-old
questions.why: Grunting, nasal flaring, and a markedly elevated respiratory rate in an infant are signs of significant respiratory distress requiring immediate reporting; the other values listed fall within normal pediatric ranges for the stated ages.

questions.q: The correct site for taking an infant's pulse when assessing during a code is:
choices: Radial artery
Brachial or femoral artery
Carotid artery
Dorsalis pedis artery
questions.why: In infants, the brachial or femoral artery is preferred for pulse checks because the short, chubby neck makes carotid palpation unreliable, unlike in older children and adults where carotid is standard during a code.

questions.q: A patient reports their pain as '10 out of 10' but is asleep when the tech checks on them. How should this be documented?
choices: Chart the 10/10 as the current status since that's what was reported earlier
Wake the patient immediately to confirm the pain score
Reassess pain when the patient wakes and document current status, noting the patient was resting/asleep at the time of the check, not in acute distress
Automatically downgrade the score to a 5 based on observed rest
questions.why: Pain should be reassessed and documented reflecting the patient's actual current status; noting that the patient is resting comfortably is clinically relevant information distinct from carrying forward an old self-reported number as if it were current.

questions.q: Tachypnea in an adult is generally defined as a respiratory rate above:
choices: 12 breaths per minute
16 breaths per minute
30 breaths per minute
20 breaths per minute
questions.why: Tachypnea is defined as a resting respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute in adults; it can be an early and sensitive sign of physiologic stress, including sepsis, pain, anxiety, or respiratory compromise.

questions.q: A patient's blood pressure differs by 20 mmHg systolic between the left and right arm. What should the tech do?
choices: Report the discrepancy; a significant interarm difference can be clinically significant and should be brought to the nurse/provider's attention
Average the two numbers and chart that as the reading
Always trust the higher reading and ignore the lower
This is a normal, expected variation that needs no follow-up
questions.why: A systolic difference of 15-20 mmHg or more between arms can be associated with vascular conditions such as aortic dissection or peripheral arterial disease and should be reported rather than averaged away or dismissed as routine variation.

questions.q: Bradycardia in an adult at rest is generally defined as a heart rate below:
choices: 50 beats per minute
60 beats per minute
70 beats per minute
80 beats per minute
questions.why: A resting adult heart rate below 60 beats per minute is defined as bradycardia; it may be a normal finding in a fit athlete but should be correlated with symptoms and other vitals before being dismissed as benign.

questions.q: When measuring an axillary temperature, the correct technique includes:
choices: Placing the probe over clothing to save time
Taking the reading immediately after the patient removes a heavy coat
Ensuring the axilla is dry and the probe tip is in direct contact with skin, arm held snug against the body for the required dwell time
Using the same technique and expecting oral-equivalent accuracy
questions.why: Axillary readings require dry skin, direct probe-to-skin contact, and the arm held against the body for the device's specified time to get a usable (though generally lower and less precise than oral or core) reading; measuring over clothing or right after heavy outerwear removal introduces error.

questions.q: A patient's oral temperature reads 36.1°C. This value is:
choices: A dangerously low hypothermic reading requiring immediate rewarming
Only acceptable if taken rectally instead
Impossible and indicates a broken thermometer
Within the low-normal range for an oral temperature (roughly 36.1-37.2°C is commonly cited as normal)
questions.why: Normal oral temperature ranges are commonly cited around 36.1-37.2°C (97-99°F), so 36.1°C sits at the low end of normal rather than representing hypothermia, which is generally defined as a core temperature below 35°C.

questions.q: For a standard 12-lead EKG, where is electrode V1 placed?
choices: 4th intercostal space, right sternal border
4th intercostal space, left sternal border
5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line
2nd intercostal space, right sternal border
questions.why: V1 goes in the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal border; V2 mirrors it at the left sternal border. Getting V1 and V2 one space too high is one of the most common precordial placement errors and can mimic anterior pathology.

questions.q: Lead V6 is correctly placed at:
choices: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line
5th intercostal space, midaxillary line, level with V4
4th intercostal space, anterior axillary line
7th intercostal space, posterior axillary line
questions.why: V6 sits at the midaxillary line, level horizontally with V4 and V5, all in the 5th intercostal space; keeping V4-V6 on the same horizontal line is key to accurate precordial placement.

questions.q: A 12-lead EKG shows limb lead artifact with an unusual rightward axis and a rhythm that looks like it could be from a different heart. The most likely cause is:
choices: Correct lead placement, this is a true finding
A normal variant with no significance
Right arm and left arm (RA/LA) lead reversal
Insufficient gel on the electrodes only
questions.why: RA/LA reversal classically produces a negative lead I and can mimic dextrocardia or an unusual axis; comparing to prior EKGs and rechecking lead placement usually resolves the confusion before assuming a true cardiac abnormality.

questions.q: For a suspected inferior STEMI, the tech should also obtain which additional leads to evaluate for right ventricular and posterior involvement?
choices: Standard 12-lead only, no additional leads needed
Additional limb leads on the legs only
Only a rhythm strip in lead II
Right-sided leads (V4R) and posterior leads (V7-V9)
questions.why: Inferior STEMI (leads II, III, aVF) has a meaningful association with right ventricular infarction and posterior involvement, so right-sided V4R and posterior V7-V9 leads are obtained to detect ST changes standard leads can miss, which changes management (e.g., avoiding nitrates in RV involvement).

questions.q: The national benchmark goal for 'door-to-EKG' time in a patient with chest pain concerning for ACS is generally:
choices: 10 minutes or less
30 minutes
60 minutes
2 hours
questions.why: Guidelines call for an EKG within 10 minutes of arrival for patients with symptoms concerning for acute coronary syndrome, since rapid identification of STEMI drives the door-to-balloon treatment timeline.

questions.q: On a rhythm strip, a regular rhythm at 150 bpm with narrow QRS complexes and no discernible P waves most likely represents:
choices: Sinus tachycardia
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)
Ventricular tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation
questions.why: SVT classically shows a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia, often around 150-250 bpm, with P waves buried or absent because the abnormal circuit is above the ventricles; sinus tachycardia usually shows visible P waves and a more gradual rate.

questions.q: Coarse, chaotic waveform with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes, or organized rhythm on the monitor most likely represents:
choices: Asystole
Atrial flutter
Ventricular fibrillation (VF)
First-degree AV block
questions.why: Ventricular fibrillation shows a chaotic, disorganized waveform of varying amplitude with no coordinated electrical or mechanical activity; it is a shockable rhythm and a cardiac arrest emergency requiring immediate activation of the code team.

questions.q: A 'sawtooth' pattern of atrial activity on the rhythm strip, often best seen in lead II, III, or aVF, is classic for:
choices: Atrial fibrillation
Third-degree heart block
Sinus arrhythmia
Atrial flutter
questions.why: Atrial flutter produces the classic sawtooth flutter waves from a reentrant atrial circuit, typically at an atrial rate around 300 bpm with a variable ventricular response depending on the AV conduction ratio (commonly 2:1 or 4:1).

questions.q: Atrial fibrillation is best described on a rhythm strip as:
choices: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible, consistent P waves
Regular rhythm with normal P waves before every QRS
Regular wide-complex rhythm at 150 bpm
A flatline with occasional QRS complexes
questions.why: Afib is defined by chaotic atrial electrical activity producing an irregularly irregular ventricular response and absence of organized P waves, distinguishing it from the regular irregularity seen in some other rhythms like sinus arrhythmia or Wenckebach.

questions.q: A rhythm strip shows progressively lengthening PR intervals until a QRS is dropped, then the pattern repeats. This describes:
choices: First-degree AV block
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach)
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz Type II
Third-degree (complete) AV block
questions.why: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) is defined by progressively lengthening PR intervals culminating in a dropped QRS, then the cycle restarts; it is usually a more benign, often reversible block compared to Mobitz II, which drops beats without PR lengthening.

questions.q: Complete disassociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with P waves marching out at their own regular rate independent of a separate, usually slower, regular QRS rate, describes:
choices: First-degree AV block
Mobitz Type II block
Third-degree (complete) heart block
Sinus arrhythmia
questions.why: Third-degree block means atrial and ventricular activity are completely dissociated, each beating at its own independent rate, because no atrial impulses conduct through the AV node; it is a high-risk rhythm often requiring pacing.

questions.q: A patient's monitor shows no electrical activity at all, a flat line, confirmed in more than one lead. This is:
choices: Ventricular fibrillation
Pulseless electrical activity
Sinus arrest
Asystole
questions.why: Asystole is the complete absence of detectable electrical (and mechanical) cardiac activity; it should be confirmed by checking in at least two leads and verifying lead/cable connections before treating it as a true code rhythm rather than equipment failure.

questions.q: Standard limb lead placement for a 4-lead or 5-lead monitor puts the black (LA) electrode:
choices: Left upper chest below the clavicle
Right upper chest below the clavicle
Right lower abdomen
Left lower abdomen or lateral chest
questions.why: Black (left arm/LA) goes on the left upper chest below the clavicle, mirroring white (RA) on the right; correct limb lead placement matters for accurate rhythm interpretation and to avoid artifact that can mimic ectopy or axis shifts.

questions.q: Which is a common cause of 60-cycle (AC) interference/artifact on an EKG tracing?
choices: Patient movement
Nearby electrical equipment or poor electrode grounding
Excessive gel on electrodes
Correct skin prep
questions.why: 60-cycle artifact appears as a fine, regular fuzzy baseline caused by nearby AC-powered equipment or poor grounding/electrode contact; it's distinct from the coarse, irregular artifact typically caused by patient movement or muscle tremor.

questions.q: Before applying EKG electrodes, proper skin prep for a diaphoretic or hairy patient includes:
choices: Applying electrodes directly over hair and sweat to save time
Using twice the usual amount of gel instead of prepping the skin
Clipping excess hair, wiping with alcohol or a dry gauze to remove oils/sweat, and lightly abrading the skin per protocol to improve conduction
Applying lotion to the skin first for better adhesion
questions.why: Good skin contact requires removing hair, oil, and moisture, and mild abrasion reduces skin impedance for a cleaner signal; skipping prep on a sweaty or hairy patient is a common cause of poor tracing quality, wandering baseline, and lead artifact.

questions.q: A wide, bizarre QRS complex tachycardia at a rate of 180, with no clear P waves, in a hemodynamically unstable patient most concerning for:
choices: Sinus tachycardia with aberrancy
Normal sinus rhythm
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Ventricular tachycardia (VT)
questions.why: A wide-complex, rapid, regular rhythm without clear P waves should be treated as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise, especially in an unstable patient, because assuming a benign cause and delaying escalation can be fatal.

questions.q: When acquiring a 12-lead EKG, the patient should be positioned:
choices: Supine, still, and relaxed with limbs not crossed, breathing normally without talking
Sitting fully upright with legs dangling
Standing to get an accurate baseline
In any comfortable position since positioning doesn't affect tracing quality
questions.why: Supine positioning with the patient still, limbs uncrossed, and not talking minimizes motion and muscle artifact; sitting upright or standing can shift the heart's position relative to the electrodes and introduce artifact, affecting tracing accuracy.

questions.q: ST-segment elevation, when significant and in the correct anatomic leads, on a 12-lead is most concerning for:
choices: Old, resolved myocardial infarction
Acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)
Normal early repolarization only, never needs review
Atrial enlargement
questions.why: New, significant ST elevation in anatomically contiguous leads is the hallmark finding used to identify STEMI and trigger rapid cath lab activation; while some ST elevation can be a benign variant, any new finding must be shown to a provider immediately, not filtered by the tech.

questions.q: Leads II, III, and aVF on a 12-lead correspond to which area of the heart?
choices: Anterior wall
Lateral wall
Inferior wall
Septal wall
questions.why: II, III, and aVF are the inferior leads, reflecting the inferior wall of the left ventricle typically supplied by the right coronary artery; ST changes localized to these leads point toward an inferior-wall event.

questions.q: Leads V1-V2 primarily reflect which area of the heart?
choices: Lateral wall
High lateral wall
Inferior wall
Septal wall
questions.why: V1 and V2 are septal leads, reflecting the interventricular septum; V3-V4 are anterior, and V5-V6 with I and aVL are lateral, which is why a full set of contiguous changes across specific lead groups helps localize the affected coronary territory.

questions.q: A patient with a permanent pacemaker has a rhythm strip showing a pacer spike before every QRS complex, each followed by a wide QRS. This is:
choices: Expected paced rhythm; pacer spikes capturing and producing a paced QRS is normal for a properly functioning device
A malfunctioning pacemaker requiring immediate intervention
Ventricular fibrillation
Third-degree block with no pacing
questions.why: Consistent pacer spikes immediately followed by a QRS (evidence of capture) is the expected appearance of a normally functioning ventricular-paced rhythm; concerning findings would be spikes without a following QRS (failure to capture) or absent spikes when the intrinsic rate is too slow (failure to pace).

questions.q: The tech notices 'muscle tremor artifact' with a fine, irregular baseline during a 12-lead acquisition on an anxious, shivering patient. The best next step is:
choices: Submit the tracing as-is without concern
Help the patient relax (warm blanket, reassurance), ensure they are not gripping the rails, and repeat the tracing if quality is poor
Increase electrode gel amount only
Discontinue the EKG entirely and cancel the order
questions.why: Muscle tremor from shivering, anxiety, or gripping the bed rails creates a fuzzy, irregular baseline that can obscure important waveforms; addressing the underlying cause (warmth, reassurance, relaxed positioning) and repeating the tracing is the appropriate fix rather than submitting a poor-quality tracing or canceling the order outright.

questions.q: A rhythm strip shows a regular rhythm, normal P wave before every QRS, but the PR interval is fixed and prolonged at 0.28 seconds (normal upper limit about 0.20 sec). This is:
choices: Normal sinus rhythm
Mobitz Type II block
First-degree AV block
Third-degree block
questions.why: First-degree AV block is a consistently prolonged but fixed PR interval (greater than 0.20 seconds) with every P wave still conducting to a QRS; it is usually benign but should still be documented and reported per protocol, especially if new.

questions.q: When placing V4, the correct location is:
choices: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line
5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line
4th intercostal space, right sternal border
5th intercostal space, midclavicular line
questions.why: V4 is placed at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line, and is used as the anchor point for placing V5 and V6 along the same horizontal line at the anterior and midaxillary lines respectively.

questions.q: A tech is prepping a patient for an EKG and the patient has a right mastectomy with lymphedema in the right arm. Which adjustment, if any, is appropriate for lead placement?
choices: Standard precordial (V1-V6) placement on the chest is unaffected by an arm condition; limb leads can be moved to the torso/shoulder area per protocol if the arm cannot be used, without changing interpretation significantly
Cancel the EKG entirely
Skip the right-sided precordial leads only
Double the number of electrodes used on the left side to compensate
questions.why: Precordial lead positions are anatomic chest landmarks independent of arm status, so V1-V6 placement proceeds normally; limb leads can be relocated onto the torso (per standard modified limb lead technique) when a true limb site can't be used, without needing to cancel the study.

questions.q: Which finding on telemetry should prompt the tech to immediately get the nurse rather than just documenting it?
choices: A stable sinus rhythm at 78 bpm
A new run of ventricular tachycardia
A normal P wave before each QRS at a rate of 82
Sinus arrhythmia that varies slightly with respiration in a young patient
questions.why: A new run of VT is a potentially life-threatening rhythm change that requires immediate escalation, unlike the other options, which describe normal or benign findings that only need routine documentation.

questions.q: The purpose of obtaining a 12-lead EKG within 10 minutes of arrival for chest pain is primarily to:
choices: Satisfy a billing requirement
Determine the patient's baseline heart rate only
Rapidly identify STEMI so the cath lab or fibrinolytic pathway can be activated as early as possible, since 'time is muscle'
Replace the need for cardiac biomarkers
questions.why: Early EKG acquisition directly drives time-sensitive STEMI recognition and treatment; delays in identifying ST elevation translate to delays in reperfusion therapy and more myocardial damage, which is why the 10-minute benchmark exists.

questions.q: A monitor shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 100 bpm with a normal, upright P wave before every QRS. This is most consistent with:
choices: Ventricular tachycardia
Atrial flutter
Junctional rhythm
Sinus tachycardia
questions.why: A regular narrow rhythm with a normal P wave preceding every QRS, at a rate above 100, is sinus tachycardia — the SA node firing faster than normal, often from fever, pain, anxiety, dehydration, or other physiologic stress rather than a primary cardiac electrical problem.

questions.q: Right arm and right leg lead reversal on a limb-lead monitor most typically produces:
choices: Significant artifact or a flatline-appearing lead II because RA and RL are adjacent limbs on the same side
No noticeable change on the tracing
A clear STEMI pattern
An obvious atrial fibrillation pattern
questions.why: RA/RL reversal often produces a very low-amplitude or flat-appearing signal in lead II specifically, since those two electrodes end up too electrically similar; recognizing this pattern helps the tech troubleshoot lead placement rather than assume a true cardiac event.

questions.q: Why are posterior leads (V7-V9) sometimes added when a 12-lead shows inferior or lateral changes without obvious anterior ST elevation but strong clinical suspicion for ACS?
choices: They are never useful and are outdated
A posterior MI can be 'electrically silent' or show only subtle reciprocal ST depression in V1-V3 on the standard 12-lead, so posterior leads directly visualize that territory
Posterior leads replace the need for troponin testing
They are only used in pediatric patients
questions.why: Because standard precordial leads face the anterior chest wall, a posterior-wall infarct can appear only as ST depression and tall R waves in V1-V3 (a mirror-image reciprocal pattern); posterior leads placed on the back give a direct view of that territory when suspicion remains high.

questions.q: Per standard order of draw for venipuncture with a butterfly and multiple tubes, which tube is generally collected FIRST when blood cultures are not being drawn?
choices: Lavender (EDTA)
Gold/SST (serum separator)
Light blue (sodium citrate)
Blood culture bottles
questions.why: When blood cultures are not part of the draw, the light blue (citrate) tube for coagulation studies is drawn first (or after a discard tube with a butterfly) to avoid contamination with additives from other tubes; blood cultures, when ordered, are always collected before any other tube.

questions.q: When blood cultures ARE ordered along with other labs, the correct order of draw is:
choices: Blood cultures are drawn last, after all other tubes
Blood cultures should be split, drawn half first and half last
It doesn't matter as long as all tubes are filled
Blood cultures are drawn first, before any other additive tubes, to minimize contamination risk
questions.why: Blood culture bottles are always collected first in the draw sequence, using a dedicated aseptic technique, to reduce the risk of contamination from needle exposure to other tube additives or repeated skin puncture.

questions.q: A lavender-top tube (EDTA) is used for which type of testing?
choices: Complete blood count (CBC) and other hematology testing
Coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT)
Blood cultures
Glucose testing only
questions.why: Lavender-top tubes contain EDTA, an anticoagulant that preserves cell morphology for hematology testing like CBCs; it is not used for coagulation studies, which require the specific citrate ratio in a light blue tube.

questions.q: The light blue top tube used for coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT) contains which additive, and why is correct fill volume critical?
choices: Heparin; fill volume doesn't matter for coag testing
Sodium citrate; the tube must be filled to the exact fill line because the citrate-to-blood ratio directly affects PT/PTT results
EDTA; underfilling has no effect on results
No additive; it's a plain tube
questions.why: Sodium citrate binds calcium to prevent clotting, and coagulation testing depends on a precise blood-to-citrate ratio; an underfilled citrate tube dilutes clotting factors relative to citrate and will falsely prolong PT/PTT results, leading to tube rejection.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common preventable cause of a hemolyzed blood sample?
choices: Using an appropriately sized needle for the vein
Inverting an EDTA tube gently 8-10 times per protocol
Drawing through a small-gauge needle with excessive suction force, or vigorously shaking the tube after collection
Using a straight venipuncture with minimal tourniquet time
questions.why: Hemolysis, the rupture of red blood cells, is commonly caused by drawing too forcefully through a needle that's too small, prolonged tourniquet time, or vigorous shaking/mixing of the sample; it can falsely elevate potassium, LDH, and other intracellular analytes, prompting rejection and redraw.

questions.q: Correct skin antisepsis technique before a blood culture draw includes:
choices: A quick alcohol wipe only, no dwell time needed
Reusing the same swab for both blood culture sites to save time
Cleaning site immediately before puncturing without any drying time
Chlorhexidine (or approved alternative) applied with proper technique and allowed to fully air dry before venipuncture
questions.why: Proper skin antisepsis (commonly chlorhexidine) requires adequate application and full air-drying time (per product, often 30 seconds or more) before puncture, since puncturing wet antiseptic can both sting and reduce its antimicrobial effect, increasing contamination risk.

questions.q: Standard practice for adult blood cultures ordered to evaluate for bacteremia typically requires:
choices: Two sets (aerobic and anaerobic bottles) from two separate venipuncture sites
One bottle from one site
A single bottle drawn from an existing IV line only
Cultures only if the patient is afebrile
questions.why: Two sets, each with an aerobic and anaerobic bottle, drawn from two different sites, improves sensitivity for detecting true bacteremia and helps distinguish a true pathogen from a skin-flora contaminant if only one set is positive.

questions.q: Underfilling a blood culture bottle below the recommended volume primarily risks:
choices: No effect on results
Reduced sensitivity for detecting true pathogens, potentially causing a false-negative culture
Automatic contamination flagging regardless of result
Overestimating bacterial growth
questions.why: Adequate blood volume (commonly around 8-10 mL per adult bottle, per manufacturer) is directly tied to the sensitivity of culture growth; underfilling dilutes the sample and lowers the chance of detecting a true pathogen even when bacteremia is present.

questions.q: Which two identifiers are acceptable for patient identification before a blood draw?
choices: Room number and bed number
Physical appearance and verbal confirmation of 'yes' to their name
Full name and date of birth, verified against the armband and the order
Insurance card only
questions.why: Two patient-specific identifiers, typically full name and date of birth, must be verified against both the patient's armband and the test order/requisition; room or bed numbers are never acceptable because patients can be moved or share a room.

questions.q: A specimen is rejected by the lab because it was labeled after leaving the patient's bedside. The correct practice is:
choices: Label tubes at a convenient time before end of shift
Labeling can be done by any staff member later, as long as it's eventually labeled
Pre-label tubes before entering the room to save time
Label every tube at the bedside, in the presence of the patient, immediately after collection, before leaving the room
questions.why: Chain-of-custody and patient safety require labeling specimens at the bedside immediately after collection and before leaving the patient, confirming the label matches the patient present; pre-labeling or delayed labeling risks a mislabeled or mismatched specimen, a leading cause of transfusion and lab errors.

questions.q: Point-of-care glucose testing quality control (QC) should be performed:
choices: Per manufacturer and facility policy, typically each shift or per defined interval, plus whenever a new reagent lot is opened
Never, POC devices don't require QC
Only if a result looks unusual
Once per month regardless of use
questions.why: Regular QC checks (commonly each shift and with new lots/strips) verify the point-of-care device is measuring accurately before patient results are trusted; skipping QC risks reporting inaccurate glucose values that could lead to inappropriate treatment.

questions.q: A point-of-care troponin result comes back markedly elevated on a chest pain patient. The tech's correct action is:
choices: Repeat the test themselves to confirm before telling anyone
Immediately report the result to the nurse or provider per critical value protocol
Document it in the chart and mention it at end of shift
Assume it's a lab error since POC troponin is rarely wrong
questions.why: Critical values, including a significantly elevated troponin, require immediate verbal reporting to the responsible nurse or provider per facility protocol, not delayed documentation or independent re-testing by the tech before notifying anyone.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid reason a specimen may be rejected by the lab?
choices: The tube was filled to the correct level
The patient was properly identified with two identifiers
The tube type doesn't match what the ordered test requires (e.g., EDTA tube sent for a coagulation study)
The specimen arrived within the required time window
questions.why: Sending the wrong tube type for the ordered test (wrong additive) invalidates the sample chemically for that assay and is a standard rejection criterion, unlike correct fill volume, proper ID, and timely transport, which are all acceptable practices.

questions.q: A clotted lavender-top (EDTA) tube submitted for a CBC will most likely result in:
choices: Acceptance and normal processing
No impact on the CBC results
Automatic correction by the lab's analyzer
Rejection, since clotting disrupts accurate cell counts and requires a redraw
questions.why: Once a sample clots, the anticoagulant failed to do its job (often from inadequate or delayed mixing after draw), and cell counts and morphology can no longer be accurately measured, so the specimen is rejected and must be redrawn.

questions.q: The gold or tiger-top tube (serum separator, SST) is commonly used for:
choices: Chemistry panels and other tests requiring serum, such as basic metabolic panel or liver function tests
Coagulation panels
Blood cultures
Hematology/CBC testing
questions.why: SST tubes contain a clot activator and gel separator, ideal for serum chemistry testing; they are not appropriate for coagulation studies (which need citrated plasma) or CBCs (which need whole blood with EDTA anticoagulant).

questions.q: Why is it important to invert an EDTA (lavender) tube gently several times immediately after collection rather than shaking it vigorously?
choices: Inverting is unnecessary; the anticoagulant mixes on its own over time
Gentle inversion mixes the anticoagulant with the blood to prevent clotting, while vigorous shaking can hemolyze red cells and invalidate the sample
Vigorous shaking improves sample quality
Only chemistry tubes need to be inverted
questions.why: Adequate but gentle mixing (typically 8-10 inversions) distributes the anticoagulant to prevent clot formation, while overly forceful shaking mechanically damages red cells, causing hemolysis that can falsify results and trigger rejection.

questions.q: A patient has an IV running dextrose in the same arm where blood is being drawn for a glucose level. The best practice is:
choices: Draw from that same arm since it's already accessed
It has no effect on lab draws
Draw from the opposite arm, or if unavoidable, draw well below/distal to the IV site and note it, since drawing near a dextrose infusion can falsely elevate glucose
Turn the IV fluids off for exactly 5 seconds and draw immediately
questions.why: Drawing blood from or near an arm receiving IV fluids, especially dextrose, risks contaminating the sample with infusate and falsely skewing results like glucose or electrolytes; the opposite arm is preferred, and any draw near an IV site should be clearly documented.

questions.q: Which best describes 'chain of custody' documentation, relevant for forensic or legal specimens (e.g., blood alcohol for law enforcement)?
choices: Not required for any ED specimens
Chain of custody only applies to urine specimens
Only the collecting tech's name needs to be recorded
A documented, unbroken record of who collected, handled, and transported the specimen at every step, required for legal defensibility
questions.why: Chain of custody requires a continuous documented record of everyone who has possession of or access to a specimen from collection through final disposition, which is essential for legal specimens to withstand challenge in court.

questions.q: A hemolyzed potassium result is likely to show:
choices: A falsely elevated value, because potassium is released from ruptured red blood cells
A falsely low value
No change from the true value
An unpredictable, random value
questions.why: Red blood cells contain far more intracellular potassium than plasma, so when cells rupture (hemolysis), that potassium is released into the sample and falsely raises the measured level, which is why hemolyzed electrolyte panels are typically rejected and redrawn.

questions.q: When performing a point-of-care glucose test, the first drop of blood from a fingerstick is often:
choices: Used for the test since it's the most accurate
Wiped away, using the second drop for testing, because the first drop can be diluted with tissue fluid or alcohol residue
Never wiped away regardless of technique
Only relevant for venous draws, not fingersticks
questions.why: Wiping the first drop away and using the second helps avoid contamination from residual alcohol or interstitial fluid, both of which can skew the glucose reading; proper technique matters for point-of-care accuracy just as it does for venous sampling.

questions.q: A tech draws blood but the tube fill is below the minimum line required for a coagulation study. The correct action is:
choices: Send it anyway and let the lab decide
Add saline to bring it up to the fill line
Recognize it will likely be rejected and redraw, since underfilled citrate tubes give inaccurate PT/PTT results
Submit it labeled 'quantity not sufficient' and move on without a redraw
questions.why: An underfilled citrate tube changes the blood-to-anticoagulant ratio and invalidates coagulation results; the correct step is to recognize the error and redraw a properly filled tube rather than sending a sample expected to be rejected or altering it with saline.

questions.q: Which of these situations is an appropriate reason to reject a urine specimen for urinalysis?
choices: The specimen was delivered to the lab within 30 minutes
The specimen was a clean-catch midstream collection
The specimen was refrigerated per protocol while awaiting pickup
The specimen container is unlabeled or the label doesn't match the requisition
questions.why: An unlabeled specimen, or one where the label and order don't match, cannot be safely verified as belonging to the correct patient and must be rejected; timely delivery, appropriate refrigeration, and correct collection technique are all acceptable practices.

questions.q: The correct order for donning personal protective equipment before performing a bedside procedure involving body fluids is generally:
choices: Gown, mask/respirator, eye protection/face shield, then gloves last
Gloves, then gown, then mask/eye protection
Mask, gloves, gown, eye protection
Order does not matter as long as everything is worn eventually
questions.why: Standard donning sequence is gown first, then mask or respirator, then eye protection or face shield, with gloves donned last so they can cover the gown cuffs; doffing generally reverses key steps, removing gloves first since they're the most contaminated.

questions.q: A tech is asked to collect a 'clean catch' midstream urine specimen instruction for a patient. The key patient instruction is:
choices: Collect the very first stream into the cup
Clean the area, begin urinating into the toilet, then move the collection cup into the stream mid-void without stopping and restarting
Hold urine for 24 hours before collecting
No cleaning is necessary if the patient showered that morning
questions.why: Clean-catch technique reduces contamination from skin flora by having the patient cleanse first, initiate voiding, and then catch a midstream sample, avoiding the initial urine stream, which carries the most contamination from the urethral opening.

questions.q: Two patient identifiers are required before specimen collection primarily to prevent:
choices: Delays in lab turnaround time
Needle-stick injuries
Wrong-patient errors, including mislabeled specimens and transfusion reactions from misidentified blood type samples
Hemolysis of the sample
questions.why: Positive patient identification with two identifiers is a core safety practice specifically designed to prevent specimen mix-ups, which can lead to serious harm such as a mistyped blood sample causing a fatal transfusion reaction.

questions.q: Which tube color is typically used for a basic metabolic panel drawn as a 'plasma' sample using a rapid-turnaround anticoagulant, common in many EDs for faster chemistry results?
choices: Lavender (EDTA)
Pink (EDTA, blood bank)
Light blue (sodium citrate)
Green (lithium or sodium heparin, often 'PST' with gel separator)
questions.why: Green-top heparin tubes (often a PST gel-separator variant) yield plasma faster than serum tubes because they don't require clotting time, which is why many EDs use them for STAT chemistry panels when speed matters.

questions.q: A pink-top (or pink/lavender-equivalent, EDTA) tube used for type and screen/crossmatch testing requires which special labeling practice at most facilities?
choices: A dedicated blood bank armband/wristband number system and handwritten bedside labeling matching that band, per facility blood bank policy
Standard labeling is sufficient, same as any other tube
No labeling is needed since the sample is discarded after typing
Only the ordering provider's name is required on the label
questions.why: Blood bank specimens for type and screen or crossmatch typically require a unique blood-bank identification band and specimen labeling system beyond the standard medical record number, because a mislabeled type and screen is one of the most dangerous possible lab errors.

questions.q: A tech notices a requisition lists 'STAT troponin' but the tube received in the lab drop area was never labeled. What is the correct next step?
choices: Guess which patient it belongs to based on the order time
The specimen cannot be processed; it must be discarded and redrawn with proper bedside labeling, since patient identity can't be verified
Label it with the name from the requisition since they were probably drawn together
Ask the next tech on shift to guess and label it
questions.why: An unlabeled specimen represents an unacceptable patient safety risk and cannot be matched to a patient reliably after the fact; policy requires discarding it and redrawing with correct bedside identification and labeling, even for a STAT test.

questions.q: Which statement about specimen transport time for a basic chemistry panel is generally accurate?
choices: Specimens can sit at room temperature indefinitely with no effect
Only hematology specimens have time-sensitive processing
Most chemistry specimens should be processed within a defined window (often around 1-2 hours) to avoid analyte degradation or cell metabolism affecting results (e.g., falsely low glucose over time)
Refrigeration always extends the allowable window indefinitely regardless of test
questions.why: Cells in a specimen continue metabolic activity after collection (for example, ongoing glycolysis lowers glucose over time), so most chemistry specimens have a defined acceptable window for processing, and delays beyond that can distort results even without visible clotting or hemolysis.

questions.q: Standard precautions during any blood draw include:
choices: Gloves only, gown and eye protection are optional
Full PPE (gown, mask, eye protection, gloves) for every single draw regardless of risk
No PPE needed for a routine venipuncture on a cooperative patient
Gloves at minimum for every draw, with additional PPE (gown, mask, eye protection) added based on anticipated splash/spray risk
questions.why: Standard precautions require gloves for any contact with blood or body fluids, with additional PPE layered on based on the anticipated risk of splash or spray (for example, a difficult draw on a combative patient); routine venipuncture on a cooperative patient doesn't automatically require full PPE.

questions.q: A tech draws a blood culture and inadvertently touches the venipuncture site with an ungloved finger after cleaning but before inserting the needle. The correct action is:
choices: Re-clean the site before proceeding, since touching after antisepsis reintroduces contamination risk (this is why 'no-touch' technique is taught)
Proceed with the draw since the skin was already cleaned
Use a different needle only, no need to re-clean
Document a note but proceed without re-cleaning
questions.why: Touching the prepped site after antisepsis, even briefly, can reintroduce skin flora and increase the risk of a contaminated culture; standard teaching is a strict 'no-touch' technique after cleaning, and if broken, the site should be re-prepped before proceeding.

questions.q: What is the primary reason for using two separate venipuncture sites when drawing paired blood cultures?
choices: It's faster than drawing from one site twice
It helps distinguish a true bloodstream infection (positive at both sites) from a contaminant (positive at only one site, often a skin organism)
One site is for aerobic, the other for anaerobic testing exclusively
Regulatory requirement with no clinical rationale
questions.why: If the same organism, especially a common skin flora like coagulase-negative staph, grows in only one of two separately drawn sites, it's more likely a contaminant; growth in both sites raises much stronger suspicion for true bacteremia, which is why two sites are standard.

questions.q: Which of the following would most likely cause a falsely low point-of-care glucose reading?
choices: Using a properly warmed, well-perfused fingertip
Wiping away the first drop of blood before testing
Testing from a cold, poorly perfused finger, or a fingertip still wet with alcohol that wasn't allowed to dry
Using a fresh test strip within its expiration date
questions.why: Residual alcohol dilutes the blood sample and can falsely lower a glucose reading, and poor peripheral perfusion from a cold extremity can also affect accuracy; letting the alcohol dry fully and choosing a warm, well-perfused site avoids both issues.

questions.q: A specimen for a stool occult blood test is contaminated with toilet bowl cleaner residue. This specimen should be:
choices: Processed as normal, cleaners don't interfere
Only a problem if the result is negative
Diluted with water before sending to correct for contamination
Rejected and recollected, since certain cleaning chemicals can cause false-positive or false-negative occult blood results
questions.why: Toilet bowl cleaners and certain chemicals can interfere with the chemical reaction used in occult blood testing, producing unreliable false-positive or false-negative results, so a clean, uncontaminated collection method (or a specific collection card) is required.

questions.q: When labeling a specimen container, which practice is correct?
choices: Fill out the label completely at the patient's bedside immediately after the specimen is obtained, confirming identifiers directly with the patient/armband at that moment
Label the container before entering the room based on the chart, then verify at bedside
It is acceptable to label using printed labels prepared the night before for a scheduled draw
Verbal confirmation from a family member alone is sufficient identification
questions.why: Correct practice labels the specimen at the bedside at the time of collection, with identifiers actively verified against the patient present (not just the chart or a label prepared in advance), which closes the gap where a wrong-patient error could occur.

questions.q: A tech notices a lab result flagged as a 'critical value' for potassium of 6.8 mEq/L. What is the required action?
choices: Chart it normally; it will be seen on the next routine review
Immediately notify the nurse or provider per critical value/panic value protocol, since this level can cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias
Wait for the ordering provider's next rounding time
Repeat the test personally before telling anyone
questions.why: A potassium this high is a recognized critical/panic value with real risk of dangerous arrhythmias including cardiac arrest, and facility policy requires immediate verbal notification to the responsible clinician, not routine or delayed communication.

questions.q: Which best describes appropriate handling of a specimen that must be kept on ice (such as an arterial blood gas)?
choices: Room temperature transport is equivalent and ice isn't necessary
Freeze the specimen solid for best accuracy
Place promptly on ice per protocol and transport quickly, since delayed or improperly stored ABG specimens can give inaccurate gas values as cellular metabolism continues
Warm the specimen to body temperature before transport
questions.why: Arterial blood gas samples are especially time- and temperature-sensitive because ongoing cellular metabolism in the syringe continues to consume oxygen and produce CO2; prompt icing (per current protocol/device) and rapid transport help preserve an accurate result.

questions.q: A tech is asked to collect a specimen for legal blood alcohol testing on a patient involved in a motor vehicle crash. Which additive tube must be avoided, and why?
choices: Gray-top (sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate) should be avoided; it's actually the preferred tube for this test
No special precautions are needed for legal blood alcohol draws
EDTA tubes must always be used regardless of policy
Alcohol-based skin antiseptics must be avoided at the collection site, since alcohol prep can contaminate the sample and affect legal defensibility
questions.why: For legal or forensic blood alcohol testing, a non-alcohol antiseptic (such as povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine) is used to clean the site instead of alcohol, since alcohol contamination could compromise the sample's evidentiary value and be challenged in court; the gray-top sodium fluoride tube is actually correct for this test because it inhibits ongoing glycolysis/fermentation.

questions.q: A gray-top tube (sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate) is most commonly used for which test?
choices: Blood glucose/lactate testing, since the additive inhibits glycolysis and preserves the sample for accurate levels
Coagulation studies
Blood cultures
CBC/hematology testing
questions.why: Sodium fluoride inhibits ongoing glycolysis by red and white blood cells in the tube, preventing a falsely low glucose (or lactate) result that would otherwise occur as cells continue consuming glucose after the draw sits waiting for processing.

questions.q: A tech is asked to collect a specimen for a rapid strep test. Correct technique includes:
choices: Swabbing only the front of the tongue
Swabbing both tonsillar pillars and the posterior pharynx firmly, avoiding the tongue and cheeks which can dilute the sample or cause false negatives
Having the patient swallow before swabbing to clear secretions first
Using a wet swab dipped in saline before collection
questions.why: An adequate rapid strep swab requires firm contact with both tonsillar areas and the posterior pharyngeal wall, since inadequate sampling (touching mostly the tongue or cheeks) is a common cause of false-negative results, not a technique variation without consequence.

questions.q: A basic splinting principle for an extremity fracture is to immobilize:
choices: Only the fracture site itself
Only the nearest joint, whichever is closer
The joint above and the joint below the injury site
The entire limb from fingertip to shoulder regardless of injury location
questions.why: Effective splinting immobilizes the joint above and the joint below the fracture to prevent movement at the fracture site from either direction; splinting only the injury site itself allows continued motion and pain at the adjacent joints.

questions.q: Before and after applying a splint, the tech must assess and document:
choices: Only the patient's pain level
Range of motion of the injured joint through full extension
Only the color of the skin
Neurovascular status distal to the injury: pulse, movement, and sensation (PMS/CSM)
questions.why: Checking pulse, movement, and sensation (or circulation, sensation, movement) distal to the injury both before and after splinting is essential to confirm the splint hasn't compromised circulation or nerve function; a splint that impairs these findings needs to be loosened or removed immediately.

questions.q: After splint application, a patient reports increasing numbness and the fingers distal to the splint are pale and cool. The correct action is:
choices: Loosen or remove the splint and reassess immediately, then notify the nurse/provider, since this suggests vascular compromise
Reassure the patient this is expected and recheck in one hour
Tighten the splint further to provide more stability
Elevate the limb and wait until end of shift to reassess
questions.why: New pallor, coolness, and numbness distal to a splint are signs of vascular or nerve compromise and require prompt loosening/removal of the splint and reassessment, with immediate notification of the team, rather than waiting or tightening further.

questions.q: Standard wound irrigation for a simple laceration prior to closure typically uses:
choices: Full-strength hydrogen peroxide to sterilize the wound
Normal saline (or potable tap water per some protocols) delivered with adequate pressure to flush debris and reduce bacterial load
Betadine solution flushed directly into the wound bed
Alcohol-based antiseptic flushed into the wound
questions.why: Normal saline (and, per some evidence-based protocols, clean tap water) is the standard irrigation fluid, delivered with enough pressure (often via a syringe with a splash guard) to mechanically remove debris and reduce contamination; hydrogen peroxide and alcohol can damage healthy tissue and are not used for wound bed irrigation.

questions.q: Which dressing type is generally appropriate for a dry, minimally draining superficial wound?
choices: A heavily absorptive alginate dressing
A wet-to-dry packing gauze
A simple non-adherent or dry gauze dressing
An occlusive hydrocolloid for a heavily draining wound
questions.why: Dry, low-drainage wounds generally do well with a simple non-adherent or dry dressing; heavily absorptive dressings like alginates and wet-to-dry packing are reserved for wounds with significant exudate or specific debridement needs, not routine dry, minor wounds.

questions.q: General guidance for suture removal timing on the face is typically around:
choices: 4-6 weeks
7-10 days
14-21 days
3-5 days
questions.why: Facial sutures are typically removed earlier, around 3-5 days, because facial skin heals quickly and has a strong cosmetic concern for minimizing suture-mark scarring; areas under more tension, like the back or over joints, are left in longer (often 10-14 days or more), varying by protocol.

questions.q: General guidance for suture removal timing over a high-tension area like the back or an extensor surface of a joint is typically around:
choices: 10-14 days or longer, per provider/protocol
7-10 days
3-5 days
Sutures over joints are never removed, only dissolvable sutures are used
questions.why: High-tension areas such as the back, over joints, or extensor surfaces need longer support before removal, generally 10-14 days or more depending on the wound and protocol, since premature removal risks wound dehiscence in areas under greater mechanical stress.

questions.q: When assisting with a Foley catheter insertion, the tech's role typically includes:
choices: Independently inserting the catheter without supervision in all cases
Gathering supplies, maintaining a sterile field, positioning/assisting the patient, and providing supplies during the procedure per facility scope
Determining catheter size based on personal preference
Deciding independently whether a catheter is medically necessary
questions.why: ED techs generally assist with Foley insertion by preparing supplies, helping maintain sterility, and positioning or supporting the patient, while insertion itself and clinical decision-making about necessity and sizing remain within nursing/provider scope unless facility policy and additional certification specifically expand tech scope.

questions.q: Before assisting with nasogastric (NG) tube placement, an important pre-procedure step is:
choices: Confirming the patient has eaten recently for lubrication purposes
Skipping measurement since all NG tubes are inserted to the same depth
Measuring the appropriate insertion length (commonly nose-to-earlobe-to-xiphoid, NEX) and having suction and confirmation methods ready
Ensuring the patient is standing during insertion
questions.why: Estimating insertion depth using a landmark method like nose-to-earlobe-to-xiphoid process (NEX) helps ensure the tube reaches the stomach appropriately; a recent meal is not a relevant prerequisite, and NG insertion is done with the patient positioned upright/sitting when possible, not standing.

questions.q: Prior to a 12-lead EKG or cardiac procedure requiring electrode placement, appropriate skin prep for a diaphoretic patient includes:
choices: Applying electrodes directly to damp skin
Skipping prep since modern electrodes work regardless of skin condition
Using extra adhesive tape over wet electrodes instead of drying the skin
Drying the skin, removing excess hair/oil as needed, and lightly abrading per protocol before electrode placement
questions.why: Proper skin prep (drying, hair removal if needed, light abrasion) reduces skin impedance and improves electrode adhesion and signal quality; applying electrodes to damp or oily skin is a common cause of poor tracing and lead artifact.

questions.q: A wound irrigation using a large syringe should deliver enough pressure to be effective while avoiding tissue damage; a commonly cited target pressure range is approximately:
choices: 5-8 psi, achievable with a 35 mL syringe and 19-gauge needle/splash-guard tip
1-2 psi, using gravity only, no syringe needed
50-60 psi using a high-pressure power washer setup
There is no meaningful target; any pressure works the same
questions.why: A widely cited effective range for wound irrigation is roughly 5-8 psi, commonly achieved using a 30-35 mL syringe with an 18-19 gauge needle or a commercial splash-guard tip; pressure that's too low won't adequately clean the wound, and pressure that's too high can damage tissue and drive debris deeper.

questions.q: When assisting with a procedure requiring a sterile field, if the tech notices a portion of the sterile drape becomes wet from an unsterile surface underneath, the correct action is:
choices: Continue since only visible contamination matters
Treat that area (and anything on it) as contaminated per strike-through principle, and notify the person performing the procedure
Dry the wet area with a sterile gauze and continue
Cover the wet spot with another sterile towel and continue as normal
questions.why: Moisture that soaks through a barrier ('strike-through') is considered to carry contamination from the unsterile surface below, so that portion of the field (and any items on it) is treated as contaminated and the team must be notified to correct it, not simply covered or dried over.

questions.q: The primary purpose of checking neurovascular status distal to a splint AFTER application (not just before) is to:
choices: Confirm the splint is aesthetically pleasing
Satisfy a purely administrative documentation requirement with no clinical value
Detect any new circulatory or nerve compromise caused by the splint itself, since swelling or an overly tight splint can develop after application
Determine if the patient needs pain medication
questions.why: Post-splinting neurovascular checks specifically catch complications the splint itself may cause, such as increasing swelling under a snug splint compromising circulation over time, which is why both pre- and post-application checks are required, not just one or the other.

questions.q: Which wound type generally requires wet-to-dry or specialized packing dressings rather than a simple dry dressing?
choices: A clean, dry superficial abrasion
A simple abrasion covered by a non-adherent dressing
A well-approximated sutured laceration with minimal drainage
A deep wound with significant necrotic tissue or heavy drainage requiring debridement/absorption
questions.why: Deep wounds with necrotic tissue or heavy exudate often need packing and more absorptive or debriding dressing strategies (such as wet-to-dry gauze per order, alginates, or other specialized products), unlike simple, dry, low-drainage wounds that do well with a basic dressing.

questions.q: When helping position a patient for a lumbar puncture, the typical positioning is:
choices: Lateral recumbent with knees drawn toward the chest and chin tucked (or sitting, leaning forward, depending on provider preference)
Standing upright, leaning forward over a table
Prone, flat on the stomach
Supine with legs elevated above the heart
questions.why: Lumbar puncture is typically performed with the patient in a lateral recumbent, fetal-like position (knees to chest, chin tucked) to open the intervertebral spaces, though some providers prefer a seated, forward-leaning position; prone and supine-with-legs-elevated are not standard LP positions.

questions.q: A tech is asked to assist with irrigation of a patient's eye after a chemical splash. The priority action is:
choices: Wait for the ophthalmology consult before starting irrigation
Begin copious irrigation immediately with saline or appropriate solution, continuing per protocol/pH check, since timely irrigation limits ongoing tissue damage
Only irrigate if the patient reports significant pain
Use full-strength antiseptic solution for irrigation instead of saline
questions.why: Chemical eye exposures are time-critical; immediate, copious irrigation (often continued until pH normalizes per protocol) limits ongoing chemical injury and should not be delayed for a specialist consult or based on the patient's pain level, which is an unreliable indicator of exposure severity.

questions.q: Which statement about assisting with incision and drainage (I&D) of an abscess is correct for an ED tech's typical scope?
choices: The tech independently performs the incision
The tech determines whether the abscess needs drainage
The tech typically assists by gathering supplies, maintaining the sterile field, and providing wound care supplies/packing materials, while the incision itself is performed by the provider
The tech administers local anesthesia independently
questions.why: I&D is a provider-performed procedure; the tech's role is generally supportive — supply gathering, maintaining sterility, assisting with positioning, and providing dressing/packing materials — not performing the incision, determining medical necessity, or administering anesthesia.

questions.q: Splinting material (such as a padded rigid splint) should extend:
choices: Exactly to the fracture site and no further
As far as possible, covering the entire limb regardless of injury location
Only halfway between the two adjacent joints
Beyond the joint above and below the injury for adequate immobilization, without impeding distal circulation checks
questions.why: Correct splint length spans past both adjacent joints to properly immobilize the fracture while still allowing fingers or toes to remain visible for ongoing neurovascular checks; splinting only to the fracture site or covering fingertips defeats proper stabilization and monitoring.

questions.q: A wound is closed with staples instead of sutures. General removal timing guidance for staples on an extremity is typically similar to sutures in that region, commonly around:
choices: 7-14 days depending on location and tension, per provider order
24-48 hours
4-6 weeks universally regardless of location
