Staples are never removed; they dissolve naturally
questions.why: Staple removal timing generally follows the same location-based logic as sutures (shorter for low-tension areas, longer for high-tension areas), commonly in the 7-14 day range, but always per the specific provider order rather than a fixed universal number, and staples are not typically dissolvable.

questions.q: The main reason to check a splinted limb's capillary refill after immobilization is to detect:
choices: Whether the patient needs a stronger analgesic
Impaired perfusion, which if present may mean the splint needs to be loosened
Whether the fracture has healed
The patient's baseline blood pressure
questions.why: Delayed capillary refill after splinting suggests impaired perfusion, often from a splint applied too tightly or worsening swelling, and is a direct indicator that the splint needs to be loosened and the limb reassessed, not something addressed with medication or unrelated vital signs.

questions.q: When preparing a patient for suture removal, which finding would prompt the tech to notify the nurse/provider before removing sutures as scheduled?
choices: The wound edges are well-approximated and healing normally
The sutures are the scheduled removal day per the chart
Signs of wound infection such as increasing redness, warmth, purulent drainage, or wound separation
The patient reports mild itching at the site, which is expected during healing
questions.why: Signs of infection (increasing redness, warmth, purulent drainage) or dehiscence (separation) are findings that need provider evaluation before proceeding with routine suture removal, unlike normal healing signs such as mild itching or well-approximated edges, which don't change the plan.

questions.q: A patient needs a peripheral IV start assisted/prepped by the tech in a state/facility where tech scope includes IV insertion under protocol. Standard technique to reduce infection risk includes:
choices: Reusing a tourniquet across multiple patients without cleaning
Skipping site prep if the patient's skin looks clean
Palpating the vein again after cleaning to confirm placement, using an ungloved finger
Cleaning the site with an appropriate antiseptic (such as chlorhexidine or alcohol) in a single-direction or circular motion, allowing it to dry, and not repalpating the site after cleaning
questions.why: Proper IV insertion antisepsis includes cleaning correctly, letting it dry, and avoiding re-palpation of the cleaned site (or using a sterile-gloved finger only if repalpation is truly necessary), since touching after prep reintroduces skin flora and raises infection risk; tourniquets are single-patient-use items in standard infection control practice.

questions.q: Assisting with wound closure using cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive ('skin glue') is generally appropriate for:
choices: Clean, low-tension, linear wounds with well-approximated edges and minimal contamination
Deep wounds under high tension
Any wound regardless of contamination or depth
Wounds actively bleeding heavily
questions.why: Tissue adhesive works best on clean, low-tension, linear wounds with edges that approximate easily; it is not appropriate for deep, high-tension, heavily contaminated, or actively bleeding wounds, which need sutures, staples, or further exploration instead.

questions.q: When assisting with a procedure that requires a time-out (such as a significant bedside procedure), the tech's role includes:
choices: Skipping the time-out if the team is busy
Actively participating in verifying patient identity, procedure, and site as part of the team-based time-out process before the procedure begins
Only watching silently without participating
Performing the time-out alone before the provider arrives
questions.why: A time-out is a team-based safety check, and all participating staff, including the tech, should actively confirm identity, procedure, and site verification before the procedure starts; skipping it or treating it as optional undermines a core safety barrier against wrong-site or wrong-patient errors.

questions.q: A patient has a laceration on a flexor surface with a deep wound and the tech is asked to prepare for possible foreign body concern. Appropriate preparation includes:
choices: Assuming no imaging is needed since it's just a cut
Applying a tight dressing immediately to avoid delay before any exploration
Being ready to assist with wound exploration/imaging as ordered (such as an x-ray for radiopaque material) since certain foreign bodies aren't visible on the surface
Removing any visible debris with bare, ungloved hands to save time
questions.why: Deep wounds with foreign body concern often need imaging (x-ray is good for glass or metal; ultrasound can help with radiolucent material like wood) and provider exploration before closure, since embedded material left behind risks infection and other complications; standard precautions (gloves) apply to any wound handling.

questions.q: The correct order for removing (doffing) PPE after a procedure involving significant blood or body fluid exposure is generally:
choices: Eye protection first, mask second, gown third, gloves last
Mask first, then gloves, then gown, then eye protection
Gown first, then everything else in any order
Gloves first, then gown, eye protection, then mask last
questions.why: Standard doffing sequence removes gloves first since they are typically the most contaminated, followed by the gown, then eye protection/face shield, with the mask or respirator removed last (and hands sanitized between steps), to minimize the risk of self-contamination during removal.

questions.q: Prior to assisting with a joint reduction procedure, an important pre- and post-procedure assessment the tech should perform is:
choices: Documenting the neurovascular status of the affected limb before and after the reduction attempt
Only checking the patient's blood pressure
Confirming the patient's insurance information
Measuring the patient's temperature only
questions.why: As with splinting and fractures, joint reductions carry a risk of neurovascular compromise, so pulse, movement, and sensation distal to the joint should be assessed and documented both before and after the procedure to catch any new deficit promptly.

questions.q: Correct technique for applying a cold pack/ice to a fresh musculoskeletal injury includes:
choices: Applying ice directly to bare skin for as long as tolerated
Wrapping the cold source in a barrier (towel/cloth) and limiting continuous application to about 15-20 minutes at a time to avoid cold injury
Leaving ice on continuously for several hours for best effect
Applying heat instead, since heat is preferred for all fresh injuries
questions.why: A barrier between ice and skin plus time-limited application (commonly around 15-20 minutes on, with breaks) reduces the risk of frostbite or cold-induced tissue injury, while direct prolonged contact or excessive duration increases that risk; heat is generally avoided in the acute phase of a fresh injury.

questions.q: A splint applied to a suspected forearm fracture should generally position the wrist in:
choices: Full flexion
Full hyperextension
A neutral or slightly functional position (often called 'position of function'), unless the injury or provider directs otherwise
Whatever position is fastest to apply, position doesn't matter
questions.why: Splinting in a neutral or slight 'position of function' (often a gentle wrist extension with fingers slightly flexed) helps maintain joint mobility and comfort during healing, unless the specific injury pattern or provider instructions call for a different position.

questions.q: A patient with a suspected open (compound) fracture has bone visibly protruding through the skin. Before splinting, the tech should ensure the provider/nurse has addressed:
choices: Nothing extra is needed; splint it exactly like a closed fracture with no other steps
Pushing the bone back under the skin before applying the splint
Washing the exposed bone with soap and water directly
Covering the wound with a sterile dressing per protocol before splinting, and documenting the open wound and neurovascular status
questions.why: An open fracture needs the exposed wound covered with a sterile dressing per protocol before splinting to reduce contamination risk, along with clear documentation of the open injury and neurovascular status; attempting to reduce or clean exposed bone is outside a tech's scope and role.

questions.q: Standard precautions apply to:
choices: All patients, regardless of diagnosis, assuming all blood and certain body fluids are potentially infectious
Only patients with a known infectious disease
Only patients undergoing invasive procedures
Only patients in isolation rooms
questions.why: Standard precautions are applied universally to every patient encounter because infectious status is often unknown; treating all blood and many body fluids as potentially infectious is the foundation of infection control, not something reserved for patients with a known diagnosis.

questions.q: The correct order for donning PPE before entering an isolation room for a patient on contact and droplet precautions is generally:
choices: Gloves, gown, mask, eye protection
Gown, mask/respirator, eye protection/face shield, gloves
Mask, eye protection, gloves, gown
Eye protection, gown, gloves, mask
questions.why: Standard donning order is gown first, then mask or respirator, then eye protection or face shield, with gloves donned last so they overlap and cover the gown cuffs; this sequence minimizes gaps in coverage during entry.

questions.q: The correct order for doffing (removing) PPE after leaving an isolation room is generally:
choices: Gown first, then gloves, then mask, then eye protection
Mask first, then gown, then gloves, then eye protection
Gloves first, then eye protection, then gown, then mask/respirator last, with hand hygiene between steps
Order doesn't matter as long as all items are removed before leaving
questions.why: Doffing removes the most contaminated items first: gloves, then eye protection/face shield, then gown, with the mask or respirator removed last (often just outside the room, after the door is closed), performing hand hygiene between steps to reduce self-contamination.

questions.q: Which of the World Health Organization's '5 moments for hand hygiene' occurs BEFORE touching a patient?
choices: After body fluid exposure risk
Before an aseptic task
After touching a patient's surroundings
Before touching a patient
questions.why: The five moments are: before touching a patient, before a clean/aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings; 'before touching a patient' is the first moment, performed on room entry before any contact.

questions.q: A used needle should be disposed of:
choices: Immediately, uncapped, into an approved puncture-resistant sharps container at the point of use, without recapping
Recapped by hand, then placed in a red sharps container
Left on the procedure tray until the end of the shift for batch disposal
Placed in the regular trash if the room doesn't have a sharps container nearby
questions.why: Needles should go directly into a sharps container at the point of use, without recapping, since recapping by hand is a leading cause of needlestick injuries; delaying disposal or using regular trash both create unnecessary exposure risk to staff.

questions.q: Per common restraint protocols modeled on Joint Commission standards, a patient in non-violent/non-self-destructive restraints generally requires reassessment and documentation at intervals of approximately:
choices: Every 15 minutes
Every 2 hours, or per specific facility policy
Once per 8-hour shift
Only when the restraint is first applied and again at discharge
questions.why: Non-violent/non-self-destructive restraint monitoring commonly requires reassessment around every 2 hours (with more frequent checks, often every 15 minutes, for violent/self-destructive restraints), though the exact interval is set by facility policy and should always be verified there.

questions.q: Per common restraint protocols, a patient in violent or self-destructive restraints typically requires neurovascular and safety checks at intervals of approximately:
choices: Once per shift
Every 4 hours
Every 15 minutes
Only if the patient requests a check
questions.why: Violent or self-destructive restraint situations carry higher acuity and risk, so monitoring intervals are typically more frequent, often around every 15 minutes, covering circulation, positioning, and psychological status, compared to the longer interval used for non-violent restraints.

questions.q: A patient identified as a fall risk should have which intervention in place?
choices: No special intervention; fall risk patients are treated the same as others
Continuous 1:1 sitter for every fall-risk patient regardless of severity
Full restraints applied automatically
Fall precautions such as bed in lowest position, call light in reach, non-slip footwear, and possibly a bed alarm, per facility protocol
questions.why: Standard fall precautions include measures like lowering the bed, keeping the call light within reach, ensuring non-slip footwear, and using bed/chair alarms as appropriate; restraints and continuous 1:1 sitters are reserved for higher-acuity situations, not applied automatically to every fall-risk patient.

questions.q: Which type of precautions (isolation category) would a patient with suspected tuberculosis require, including a fit-tested respirator for staff?
choices: Airborne precautions, using an N95 or higher-level respirator and a negative pressure room when available
Droplet precautions only
Contact precautions only
Standard precautions only, no additional isolation needed
questions.why: TB is spread via small airborne particles that can remain suspended and travel further than droplets, requiring airborne precautions: a fit-tested N95 (or higher) respirator for anyone entering the room and, ideally, a negative-pressure isolation room, which is a higher level of protection than droplet or contact precautions alone.

questions.q: A patient with confirmed influenza is placed on which type of precautions?
choices: Airborne precautions with N95 required for all staff
Droplet precautions, generally requiring a surgical mask within about 3-6 feet of the patient
Contact precautions only, no mask needed
No precautions beyond standard are needed for influenza
questions.why: Influenza is spread by larger respiratory droplets that don't typically travel or linger like true airborne pathogens, so droplet precautions (surgical mask within close proximity, per facility distance policy) are used rather than the N95/airborne protocol reserved for diseases like TB, measles, or varicella.

questions.q: A patient with a known MRSA wound infection requires which precaution category, in addition to standard precautions?
choices: Airborne precautions
Droplet precautions
Contact precautions, using gown and gloves for room entry
No additional precautions beyond standard
questions.why: MRSA and similar organisms spread through direct or indirect contact (skin-to-skin or contaminated surfaces/equipment), so contact precautions requiring gown and gloves for anyone entering the room are used, distinct from the respiratory-focused droplet and airborne categories.

questions.q: Proper isolation signage on a patient's door serves primarily to:
choices: Identify the patient's diagnosis to any passerby in the hallway for convenience
Indicate billing status for the room
Replace the need for staff to review the chart
Alert staff and visitors to required precautions and PPE before entry, protecting against transmission
questions.why: Isolation signage is a visual cue reminding everyone approaching the room what precautions and PPE are required before entry, functioning as a real-time safety barrier; while it does reflect precaution status, its core purpose is prevention of transmission, not diagnosis disclosure for convenience or billing.

questions.q: Recognizing early warning signs of escalating agitation in a patient (clenched fists, pacing, raised voice, invading personal space) should prompt the tech to:
choices: Use de-escalation techniques (calm tone, non-threatening posture, maintaining exit access) and alert the team early, before the situation worsens
Ignore it unless the patient becomes physically violent
Immediately call security to physically restrain the patient without attempting verbal de-escalation first
Match the patient's tone and volume to show they are being heard
questions.why: Early recognition allows verbal de-escalation (calm tone, respectful language, maintaining a safe distance and clear exit path) and early team notification, which can often prevent escalation to a physical confrontation; matching an agitated tone or jumping straight to physical restraint without attempting de-escalation increases risk for everyone.

questions.q: When engaging with a potentially violent patient, which positioning principle is correct for staff safety?
choices: Stand directly in front of the patient, blocking the doorway
Position yourself with a clear path to the exit and avoid being cornered or blocking your own escape route
Turn your back to the patient to appear non-threatening
Stand as close as possible to appear confident and in control
questions.why: Maintaining an accessible exit and never allowing yourself to become cornered is a core personal safety principle when dealing with a potentially violent patient; blocking your own exit, turning your back, or standing unnecessarily close all increase personal risk.

questions.q: Which of the following is an appropriate use of a chemical restraint versus a physical restraint, in general principle?
choices: Chemical restraints are always preferred over physical restraints in every situation
Chemical restraints require no monitoring once administered
The choice between chemical and physical restraint (or neither) should be based on the specific clinical situation and ordered/directed per protocol, using the least restrictive effective option
Physical restraints never require an order, only chemical restraints do
questions.why: Restraint decisions, chemical or physical, should follow the principle of using the least restrictive intervention effective for the situation, guided by clinical judgment and orders/protocol; both restraint types require ongoing monitoring and documentation, and neither is a default 'always preferred' choice.

questions.q: A sharps injury (needlestick) occurs to a tech during a procedure. The immediate correct action is:
choices: Finish the task first, then report it at the end of the shift
Ignore it if the patient has no known bloodborne disease history
Apply alcohol only, no need to report if the needle looked clean
Stop, wash the area with soap and water, and report the exposure immediately per facility protocol for evaluation and possible prophylaxis
questions.why: Needlestick injuries require immediate wound care (washing with soap and water) and prompt reporting through the facility's exposure protocol so risk can be assessed and time-sensitive interventions like post-exposure prophylaxis can be considered without delay; delaying reporting can reduce the effectiveness of these interventions.

questions.q: Which hand hygiene method is preferred when hands are visibly soiled or after caring for a patient with suspected C. difficile?
choices: Soap and water, since alcohol-based sanitizer is not reliably effective against C. difficile spores and doesn't remove visible soiling
Alcohol-based hand sanitizer only
Hand sanitizer followed immediately by gloving with no washing
No hand hygiene needed if gloves were worn throughout
questions.why: Alcohol-based hand rubs do not reliably kill C. difficile spores, and visibly soiled hands need mechanical removal of debris, so soap and water handwashing is specifically required in these situations rather than relying on alcohol-based sanitizer alone.

questions.q: A tech is assigned to care for a patient under droplet precautions and needs to transport them to radiology. The correct approach is:
choices: Transport without a mask on the patient since the tech is masked
Place a surgical mask on the patient (if tolerated) during transport and notify the receiving department of the precaution status ahead of time
Cancel the transport entirely since droplet patients can never leave their room
Only notify radiology after the patient arrives
questions.why: Masking the patient (when tolerated) during transport helps contain droplet spread outside the room, and advance notification lets the receiving department prepare appropriately, which is standard practice rather than refusing transport altogether or notifying only after arrival.

questions.q: The correct disposal method for a blood-soaked gauze dressing removed during wound care is:
choices: Regular trash, since it's just gauze
Sharps container, since any medical item goes there
Biohazard/regulated medical waste ('red bag') disposal, following facility policy for items saturated with blood or body fluid
Recycling bin, since gauze is a fabric material
questions.why: Items saturated or dripping with blood or body fluid meet the threshold for regulated medical waste ('red bag') disposal per most facility policies, distinct from sharps containers (reserved for sharp items) and regular trash (reserved for non-contaminated waste).

questions.q: Which statement about restraint documentation is accurate?
choices: Only the initial order needs to be documented; ongoing checks don't require separate documentation
Restraint use never requires a time-limited order
Documentation is only required if the patient is injured while restrained
Ongoing monitoring, including neurovascular checks, behavior, and continued need for restraint, must be documented at the required interval throughout the duration of use
questions.why: Restraint use requires an order that is time-limited and requires renewal, plus ongoing documented monitoring at defined intervals covering safety, neurovascular status, and continued clinical justification for the restraint, not just a one-time note at initiation.

questions.q: A patient in the waiting room becomes verbally aggressive but has not made any physical threats. The tech's most appropriate first response is:
choices: Use calm, respectful verbal de-escalation, involve triage/security as appropriate per protocol, and avoid engaging in an argument
Immediately call for a physical restraint team
Argue back to assert authority
Ignore the behavior and hope it resolves on its own
questions.why: Verbal aggression without physical threat generally calls for verbal de-escalation techniques first, with security or additional staff looped in per protocol if needed, rather than skipping straight to physical intervention or, at the other extreme, ignoring a situation that could escalate.

questions.q: Which of these best describes 'transmission-based precautions' as distinct from 'standard precautions'?
choices: They are the same thing with different names
Transmission-based precautions are additional measures (contact, droplet, airborne) layered on top of standard precautions for specific known or suspected pathogens
Transmission-based precautions replace the need for standard precautions
Transmission-based precautions only apply to surgical patients
questions.why: Standard precautions apply to every patient encounter; transmission-based precautions (contact, droplet, airborne) are added on top when a specific pathogen with a known transmission route is suspected or confirmed, layering extra protection rather than substituting for standard precautions.

questions.q: Sharps container replacement should occur when the container is filled to approximately what capacity, per standard safety guidance?
choices: 100% full, filled completely to the very top
Only when visibly overflowing with sharps sticking out
About 3/4 full (commonly marked with a fill line), to avoid overfilling and needlestick risk during disposal
Sharps containers are reused indefinitely and never replaced
questions.why: Sharps containers should be replaced at about the 3/4-full mark (usually indicated by a fill line on the container) to prevent overfilling, which increases the risk of a needlestick injury when someone tries to force one more item in or when the container is being handled for replacement.

questions.q: A tech notices a colleague reusing a single alcohol prep pad across two different patients' IV sites. This is:
choices: Acceptable, since it's just alcohol
Acceptable if the pad still appears clean
Only a problem if either patient has a known infection
Not acceptable; single-use items must not be reused between patients, and this should be corrected/reported per facility policy
questions.why: Single-use supplies, including prep pads, must never be reused on a different patient regardless of appearance, since visual cleanliness doesn't reflect microbial contamination; this is a patient safety issue that should be corrected in the moment and reported per policy.

questions.q: Personal protective equipment selection for a patient actively vomiting with a suspected norovirus infection should include, at minimum:
choices: Gloves and gown, given the contact transmission risk and potential for soiling from body fluids
Gloves only
No PPE is needed since norovirus is airborne only
A fit-tested N95 respirator is always required
questions.why: Norovirus spreads primarily via the fecal-oral route and contact with contaminated surfaces or body fluids, so gloves and gown for contact precautions are the minimum appropriate PPE; it is not classified as requiring airborne precautions or a fit-tested respirator.

questions.q: Which best describes appropriate use of a gait belt to prevent falls during ambulation?
choices: Gait belts are optional and rarely useful
A properly applied gait belt gives staff a secure hand-hold to assist and stabilize an at-risk patient during transfers or ambulation, reducing fall risk
Gait belts should be applied as tightly as possible around the neck for control
Gait belts replace the need for any other fall precautions
questions.why: A gait belt applied snugly around the waist (never the neck) gives staff a secure grip point to assist and catch a patient during ambulation or transfers, functioning as one part of a broader fall-prevention approach rather than a complete replacement for other precautions.

questions.q: The primary purpose of a 'sharps safety' program including safety-engineered devices (such as needles with retractable or shielded tips) is to:
choices: Make procedures take longer for no clinical benefit
Reduce the cost of sharps disposal only
Reduce needlestick injuries and associated bloodborne pathogen exposure risk to healthcare workers
Eliminate the need for a sharps container
questions.why: Safety-engineered sharps devices are specifically designed to reduce accidental needlestick injuries, which are a major route of occupational bloodborne pathogen exposure (HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C) for healthcare workers; they don't eliminate the need for proper sharps disposal.

questions.q: A patient under contact precautions for a wound infection needs a wheelchair for transport. Correct practice is:
choices: Use a wheelchair from another unit without cleaning it afterward
Equipment used for a contact-precaution patient should never be reused, only discarded
No special handling of equipment is needed under contact precautions
Use a dedicated/dedicated-for-use wheelchair when possible, or thoroughly disinfect shared equipment per protocol after use before it's used for another patient
questions.why: Under contact precautions, shared equipment either should be dedicated to that patient when feasible or thoroughly disinfected per facility protocol immediately after use before being used for another patient, preventing indirect contact transmission via contaminated equipment.

questions.q: Workplace violence prevention training generally emphasizes which principle for de-escalating a verbally hostile patient or visitor?
choices: Active listening, maintaining a calm tone and non-confrontational body language, and offering choices where possible
Raising your voice to match theirs so they know you're serious
Immediately threatening to call police for any raised voice
Standing with arms crossed and direct, unbroken eye contact to assert dominance
questions.why: Effective de-escalation relies on active listening, calm tone, open non-threatening body language, and offering reasonable choices to help the person regain a sense of control, rather than mirroring hostility, making premature threats, or using confrontational body language that can escalate tension.

questions.q: A tech is asked to help apply a restraint on an agitated but not-yet-violent patient before less restrictive measures have been tried. The appropriate response is:
choices: Apply the restraint immediately since a request was made
Voice the concern that less restrictive alternatives should be attempted first per the least-restrictive-intervention principle, and confirm there is an appropriate order before proceeding
Refuse to participate in restraint application under any circumstance
Apply the restraint but do not document anything about it
questions.why: Restraint use is generally expected to follow a least-restrictive-intervention approach and requires an appropriate order; a tech asked to skip that step appropriately raises the concern rather than either blindly complying or refusing to ever assist with a properly ordered restraint.

questions.q: In the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), a patient requiring immediate life-saving intervention is triaged as:
choices: ESI Level 5
ESI Level 3
ESI Level 1
ESI Level 4
questions.why: ESI Level 1 is reserved for patients who require immediate life-saving intervention (e.g., not breathing, no pulse, unresponsive requiring immediate intervention); it represents the highest acuity and is seen immediately, not queued behind other patients.

questions.q: A patient is triaged as ESI Level 2. This generally means:
choices: The patient can safely wait several hours to be seen
The patient needs no resources and can be discharged from triage
The lowest acuity level in the ESI system
A high-risk situation, severe pain/distress, or a patient who should not wait, needing to be seen very quickly though not requiring an immediate life-saving intervention
questions.why: ESI Level 2 identifies high-risk patients (concerning vital signs, severe pain/distress, or a situation like new confusion or chest pain) who don't yet meet Level 1 criteria but should not wait in the general queue, requiring prompt placement and evaluation.

questions.q: ESI triage levels 3, 4, and 5 are primarily differentiated from each other based on:
choices: The number of hospital resources (tests, procedures) the patient is anticipated to need, combined with vital sign considerations for level 3
Patient age only
Insurance status
Time of arrival only
questions.why: For patients not meeting Level 1 or 2 criteria, ESI uses a resource-based algorithm: Level 3 patients are expected to need two or more resources (with a vital sign check), Level 4 patients need one resource, and Level 5 patients need none, guiding relative urgency and expected workup complexity.

questions.q: SBAR, used for handoff communication, stands for:
choices: Symptoms, Behavior, Action, Response
Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
Status, Background, Analysis, Result
Setting,باckground, Assessment, Review
questions.why: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is a structured communication framework used to give a clear, organized handoff so the receiving team quickly understands what's happening, relevant history, current assessment, and what's being asked of them.

questions.q: Closed-loop communication during a critical event means:
choices: The sender repeats the instruction multiple times until someone responds
Only the team leader speaks during the event
The receiver repeats back the instruction to confirm understanding, and the sender confirms that repeat-back is correct
Communication happens only through written orders, never verbally
questions.why: Closed-loop communication requires the receiver to verbally repeat back what was heard (e.g., 'giving epinephrine 1mg IV now') and the sender to confirm it's correct, which reduces the risk of a missed or misunderstood instruction during high-stress, time-critical situations.

questions.q: A tech disagrees with a clinical decision made by a more senior team member during a critical situation and believes patient safety is at risk. The appropriate action is:
choices: Say nothing and comply, since the senior person outranks the tech
Refuse to participate in any part of the patient's care going forward
Wait until after the shift to bring it up privately
Voice the concern clearly and respectfully in the moment, and use the chain of command if the concern isn't addressed
questions.why: A speak-up culture expects any team member who identifies a safety concern to voice it clearly in real time, and to escalate through the chain of command if it isn't adequately addressed, rather than staying silent, delaying the concern until later, or disengaging from patient care entirely.

questions.q: Two patient identifiers used consistently at every point of care (medication administration, specimen collection, procedures) primarily serve to:
choices: Prevent wrong-patient errors across all aspects of care, a core patient safety practice
Speed up documentation
Satisfy a purely administrative, non-clinical requirement
Reduce the number of required signatures on forms
questions.why: Consistent two-identifier verification (commonly name and date of birth) at every care point is a fundamental safety practice specifically aimed at preventing mix-ups between patients, whether during medication administration, specimen collection, or procedures.

questions.q: Timely documentation of vital signs and interventions in the ED is important primarily because:
choices: It looks better on a performance review
Real-time, accurate documentation supports clinical decision-making, continuity of care, and legal/medical record accuracy
Documentation timing has no real clinical impact as long as it's eventually entered
Only physician documentation timing matters for patient care
questions.why: Documenting close to the time an event or vital sign occurs (rather than batching or backdating later) ensures the record accurately reflects the patient's condition and the care given, which directly supports clinical decisions made by the rest of the team and the legal integrity of the chart.

questions.q: 'Boarding' in the ED context refers to:
choices: Patients waiting in the waiting room before triage
The process of registering a patient at arrival
Admitted patients who remain in the ED, often on stretchers/hallway beds, because no inpatient bed is available yet
A type of triage documentation form
questions.why: Boarding describes admitted patients who stay in the ED, sometimes for extended periods, because an inpatient bed isn't yet available; it's a significant driver of ED crowding and throughput problems, distinct from the initial waiting-room or triage/registration process.

questions.q: Which of the following is a typical component of ED patient throughput that a tech directly supports?
choices: Setting hospital-wide bed capacity policy
Determining hospital-wide staffing ratios
Negotiating with insurance companies
Timely and accurate vital sign collection, specimen collection, and communication of results/changes to the care team, which keeps the care process moving
questions.why: Techs directly influence throughput by performing timely vitals, specimen collection, and prompt communication of findings, all of which keep the diagnostic and treatment process moving efficiently; broader system-level decisions like bed policy or staffing ratios are outside the tech's role.

questions.q: A patient triaged as ESI Level 2 for 'new onset confusion' should be:
choices: Placed promptly per Level 2 protocol, since new altered mental status is a high-risk presentation that should not wait
Placed in the general queue behind lower-acuity patients since confusion alone isn't urgent
Reassessed only if family requests it
Downgraded automatically if vitals are normal
questions.why: New-onset confusion is a recognized high-risk chief complaint under ESI criteria (it can signal stroke, sepsis, metabolic derangement, and more), warranting Level 2 assignment and prompt placement regardless of otherwise normal vital signs.

questions.q: When giving an SBAR handoff about a patient with worsening vital signs, the 'Recommendation' portion should include:
choices: A summary of the patient's entire medical history
What the tech thinks should happen next, such as a request for the nurse to reassess or notify the provider
Only the current vital signs with no further comment
The patient's insurance and demographic information
questions.why: The recommendation portion of SBAR states clearly what the communicator is asking for or suggesting (e.g., 'please come reassess, I'm concerned about this trend'), giving the receiving person a clear action item rather than just raw data without direction.

questions.q: A patient's condition changes significantly while boarding in the ED awaiting an inpatient bed. The tech's correct action is:
choices: Wait for the inpatient team to notice at the next scheduled rounding time
Assume the inpatient unit has already been alerted automatically
Notify the ED nurse/provider promptly, since the patient remains an ED patient under ED staff responsibility until physically transferred
Document the change only, without verbal notification
questions.why: A boarding patient remains under the responsibility of the ED care team until an actual physical transfer occurs, so any significant change must be reported promptly to ED staff just as it would be for any other ED patient, not assumed to be someone else's responsibility.

questions.q: Chain of command in a hospital setting exists primarily to:
choices: Limit who is allowed to speak during an emergency
Replace the need for direct communication between team members
Determine pay grade differences between staff
Provide a clear escalation pathway when a concern isn't resolved at the initial level, ensuring patient safety issues get appropriate attention
questions.why: Chain of command gives staff, including techs, a structured way to escalate an unresolved safety concern to the next appropriate level of authority, ensuring concerns don't get dropped; it exists to support safety, not to silence initial communication or serve as a pay structure.

questions.q: A tech receiving a verbal order for a task should:
choices: Use closed-loop communication: repeat the order back to confirm accuracy before carrying it out
Carry out the order exactly as heard without repeating it back
Only accept written orders, never verbal ones under any circumstance
Ask a different staff member to confirm instead of the person who gave the order
questions.why: Repeating a verbal order back to the person who gave it (closed-loop communication) confirms it was heard correctly before it's acted on, catching potential errors immediately rather than relying on a written-order-only policy that isn't realistic in fast-moving ED situations.

questions.q: ESI Level 1 criteria include patients who are, for example:
choices: Ambulatory with a minor ankle sprain
In cardiac arrest or requiring immediate airway/breathing intervention
Stable and requesting a work note
Requesting a refill of a chronic home medication
questions.why: ESI Level 1 is defined by the need for immediate life-saving intervention, such as cardiac arrest, apnea, or severe respiratory distress requiring immediate airway management; the other examples listed represent low-acuity presentations far from Level 1 criteria.

questions.q: A tech overhears a nurse and physician disagreeing loudly at the bedside about the next step for an unstable patient, creating confusion about who is directing care. The most appropriate tech action is:
choices: Pick a side and start following whichever instruction came first
Leave the room to avoid the conflict
Seek clarification on who is the designated team leader/decision-maker for the moment and confirm the current plan before acting
Perform tasks from both sets of instructions simultaneously
questions.why: In moments of unclear direction, clarifying who has decision-making authority in that moment and confirming the current plan prevents duplicated or conflicting actions; leaving, guessing, or trying to follow contradictory instructions simultaneously all risk patient harm.

questions.q: Timely documentation in the ED is generally expected to occur:
choices: At the very end of the shift, all at once
Whenever convenient, with no expectation of timeliness
Only when specifically requested by the charge nurse
As close to real-time as possible, ideally immediately after the vital sign, intervention, or observation occurs
questions.why: Real-time or near-real-time documentation is the standard expectation because it most accurately reflects when events actually occurred, supports timely clinical decisions by the rest of the team, and reduces the risk of errors or omissions that come from trying to recall details later.

questions.q: Which best describes the relationship between ESI level and expected hospital resource use for Levels 3-5?
choices: Level 3 patients are generally expected to need two or more resources, Level 4 patients one resource, and Level 5 patients no additional resources
Level 3 needs zero resources, Level 5 needs the most
Resource use has no bearing on ESI level assignment for 3-5
All three levels are assigned solely based on age
questions.why: For non-immediately-life-threatening patients, ESI uses anticipated resource needs (labs, imaging, IV fluids/meds, specialty consult, procedures) as the key differentiator: two-plus resources for Level 3, one for Level 4, and none for Level 5, alongside a danger-zone vital sign check for Level 3.

questions.q: A family member insists their loved one 'needs to be seen right now' in a busy ED waiting room, though the patient's ESI level and vitals are stable. The appropriate tech response is:
choices: Immediately move the patient ahead of higher-acuity patients to avoid conflict
Calmly explain the triage process, reassess if there's any new change in condition, and involve the triage nurse/charge nurse as appropriate
Argue with the family member about hospital policy
Ignore the family member entirely without any acknowledgment
questions.why: A calm explanation of how triage prioritization works, combined with a genuine reassessment for any new or worsening findings and looping in the triage or charge nurse as needed, respects both patient safety (accurate re-triage if warranted) and family concerns, without simply bypassing the acuity-based system or dismissing the concern.

questions.q: The primary reason ESI (or similar triage systems) exists is to:
choices: Determine billing codes at registration
Assign patients to rooms based on insurance type
Rapidly sort patients by acuity and anticipated resource need so the sickest patients are identified and treated first
Replace the need for a full nursing assessment
questions.why: Triage systems like ESI exist to quickly stratify incoming patients by how sick they are and what they're likely to need, ensuring the most critical patients are identified and prioritized rather than seen strictly in arrival order; it doesn't determine billing or replace a full nursing assessment, which still follows.

questions.q: A tech notices a discrepancy between the chief complaint documented at triage and what the patient is now describing to them at the bedside. The correct action is:
choices: Ignore it since triage already documented a complaint
Assume the patient is confused and disregard the new information
Change the triage documentation directly without discussion
Communicate the new/updated information to the nurse promptly, since it may change the clinical picture or urgency
questions.why: New or changed symptom information can meaningfully affect the clinical picture and potentially the patient's acuity, so it should be promptly communicated to the nurse rather than ignored, dismissed, or unilaterally used to alter someone else's documentation.

questions.q: Which is an example of effective closed-loop communication during a trauma resuscitation?
choices: The team leader orders '2 liters of normal saline wide open,' the tech repeats 'giving 2 liters normal saline wide open,' and the team leader confirms 'correct'
The team leader gives an order and moves on without waiting for a response
The tech silently begins the task without acknowledging the order
The order is written on a whiteboard only, with no verbal exchange
questions.why: This exchange demonstrates the full closed-loop cycle: order given, order repeated back verbatim by the receiver, and explicit confirmation by the sender, which is the standard taught for high-acuity, time-critical communication to minimize the chance of a misheard or misunderstood instruction.

questions.q: A tech is asked to escalate a concern about a patient's deteriorating condition, but the assigned nurse is busy with another critical patient. The appropriate next step is:
choices: Wait until the nurse is free, however long that takes
Escalate to another available nurse, charge nurse, or provider immediately, since patient deterioration cannot wait for a single busy staff member
Handle the deterioration independently without notifying anyone
Document it and address it only at the next scheduled check
questions.why: When the assigned nurse is unavailable, the concern should be escalated to whoever is available and appropriate (another nurse, charge nurse, provider) without delay, since patient deterioration is time-sensitive and shouldn't wait on a single person's availability.

questions.q: The 'situation' component of an SBAR handoff should concisely communicate:
choices: The patient's entire chart history
Only the patient's vital signs from the last 24 hours
Who the patient is and the current problem/reason for the communication, in a brief, focused statement
The names of everyone who has cared for the patient today
questions.why: The situation statement opens the handoff with a brief, focused identification of the patient and the immediate reason for the communication (e.g., 'Mr. Smith in bed 4, his heart rate just jumped to 150 and he's diaphoretic'), setting context quickly rather than delivering a full history upfront.

questions.q: Regarding patient identification during a code/critical event with multiple team members present, best practice is:
choices: Assume everyone already knows which patient is which since it's an emergency
Only the physician needs to confirm patient identity during a code
Skip identification checks entirely during codes to save time
Continue verifying patient identity for any patient-specific action (like medication or blood product administration) even during a high-stress critical event
questions.why: Even in the chaos of a code, patient-specific actions like medication or blood product administration still require identity verification, because the consequences of a wrong-patient error (e.g., wrong blood type transfusion) can be just as severe, or more so, during a critical event as during routine care.

questions.q: A tech notices the ED is significantly overcrowded with multiple boarding patients holding hallway beds. Which action is within the tech's role to help support throughput?
choices: Continuing to perform timely vitals, promptly reporting changes, and communicating clearly with the team so care processes for all patients keep moving efficiently
Independently deciding which patients get inpatient beds first
Refusing to care for boarding patients since they are 'someone else's problem'
Telling patients directly when they will get a bed upstairs, based on personal guesses
questions.why: During crowding, a tech's meaningful contribution to throughput is maintaining timely, accurate task completion and clear communication for every assigned patient, including those boarding; bed assignment decisions and giving patients specific timing promises are outside tech scope and can create false expectations.

questions.q: Which best distinguishes 'closed-loop communication' from simply acknowledging an order with 'okay'?
choices: There is no real difference between the two
Closed-loop requires the receiver to state back the specific content of the order, not just a general acknowledgment, so the sender can confirm accuracy
'Okay' is always sufficient in a busy ED
Closed-loop communication is only used in writing, never verbally
questions.why: A vague 'okay' doesn't confirm what was actually heard or understood, while closed-loop communication requires repeating the specific content back, allowing the sender to catch and correct any misunderstanding immediately, which is the entire safety value of the technique.

questions.q: A tech overhears the triage nurse assign an ESI level that seems inconsistent with the patient's reported symptoms (for example, crushing chest pain triaged as Level 4). The appropriate action is:
choices: Say nothing since triage decisions are outside the tech's role entirely
Re-triage the patient personally to the level the tech believes is correct
Respectfully bring the observation to the triage nurse or charge nurse's attention so the acuity can be reviewed
Wait until the patient's condition worsens before saying anything
questions.why: Any team member who notices a potential mismatch between presentation and assigned acuity should speak up to the appropriate person for review, consistent with a safety culture that values catching errors early; a tech shouldn't independently change someone else's triage assignment, but also shouldn't stay silent or wait for harm to occur.

questions.q: Which best describes appropriate 'read-back' verification when receiving a critical lab value over the phone from the lab?
choices: Simply saying 'got it, thanks' and hanging up
Assuming the value is correct since it came from the lab system
Asking the lab to send it in writing instead and skipping verbal confirmation
Writing down the value and reading it back to the caller for confirmation before ending the call
questions.why: Reading a critical value back to the caller (a form of closed-loop communication) confirms it was transcribed and heard correctly before the call ends, protecting against transcription errors on time-sensitive values that will drive immediate clinical decisions.
